verse.text: In the beginning was the Logos, and the Logos was with God, and the Logos was God.
verse.note: Nearly all translations render this “Word.” The Greek term covered speech, message, account and reason, and to many Greek-speaking readers it also suggested the rational principle that orders the world. Most scholars think John’s main background is the Hebrew Bible: God’s creating speech in Genesis 1, the “word of the Lord,” and the figure of Wisdom, which “Word” reflects and “Logos” does not. The Greek term is kept here as a title because “the Word” in current English usually means the Bible, which would give “the Word was God” a false sense.

verse.text: He was in the beginning with God.
All things came into being through him, and apart from him not one thing came into being. What has come into being

note.traditional: without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, and these words can close the sentence of verse 3 (“not one thing came into being that has come into being. In him was life”) or open the next one. Most English versions take the first option. The Greek edition translated here, like many early Christian readers, takes the second, and the translation follows it; scholars remain divided.

verse.text: in him was life, and the life was the light of humanity.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.
verse.note: The verb means to seize or overtake, and by extension to grasp with the mind. Older versions chose “comprehended”; most modern ones choose “overcome,” which fits John’s later use of the same verb for darkness overtaking a person (12:35). John may intend both senses.

verse.text: There came a man sent from God; his name was John.
He came to give testimony, to testify about the light, so that all might believe through him.
He was not the light, but came to testify about the light.
The true light, which gives light to every person, was coming into the world.

note.traditional: which lighteth every man that cometh into the world

verse.note: The words “coming into the world” can describe the light, as translated here, or “every person” (“which gives light to every person who comes into the world”). Most modern translations and scholars prefer the first, since John repeatedly speaks of Jesus as the one who comes into the world.

verse.text: He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him.
He came to what was his own, and his own people did not receive him.
But to all who did receive him he gave the right to become children of God—to those who believe in his name,
who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.
And the Logos became flesh and made his dwelling among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
verse.note: The verb is related to the ordinary word for a tent, which in the Greek Old Testament is also the word for the tabernacle, where God’s glory was present among Israel in the wilderness. Coming just before “we saw his glory,” the verb very probably carried that association for a reader who knew the Scriptures in Greek.

The traditional “only begotten” assumes the word is built on “beget,” but in period usage it means the only one of its kind, and especially an only child. “One and only” is the mainstream modern rendering, though a minority of scholars have recently defended “only begotten.” The word “Son” is supplied in English; the Greek could also be read as a general comparison, “as of a father’s only son.”

verse.text: (John testifies about him and cries out, saying, “This was the one of whom I said, ‘The one coming after me has come to be ahead of me, because he was before me.’”)
For from his fullness we have all received—grace in place of grace.
verse.note: Most translations have “grace upon grace” or “grace for grace,” picturing gifts piled one on another. In the Greek of the period, however, the preposition normally means “in place of” or “in exchange for,” and a sense of accumulation is hard to document. On this reading one gift of grace succeeds another, which may be explained by the next verse: the Law through Moses, then grace and truth through Jesus Christ. Many scholars still prefer the traditional sense.

verse.text: For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
No one has ever seen God. The one and only, himself God, who is at the Father’s side—he has made him known.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “one and only God”; most later manuscripts read “the one and only Son,” which is what the traditional English versions translate. Most editors judge “God” original because it is the harder reading and has the oldest support. The Greek can be taken as “the one and only God” or, as here, as “the one and only” with “God” added in apposition.

verse.text: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jewish leaders sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”
verse.note: The Greek says simply “the Jews,” and most translations keep that. Here the group is one with authority to send priests and Levites from Jerusalem, so John means the authorities there and not the Jewish people as a whole, to which John the Baptist, Jesus and the disciples all belonged. Scholars are divided on how best to render the word in John; some prefer “Judeans” throughout.

verse.text: He confessed and did not deny it; he confessed, “I am not the Messiah.”
verse.note: The Greek word means “anointed” and translates the Hebrew term behind “Messiah,” the anointed king Israel expected. Where it is a title under discussion, as here, “Messiah” conveys what a first-century Jewish hearer understood; “Christ” is kept where it functions as part of Jesus’s name, as in verse 17. Several modern translations make the same distinction. In verse 41 John gives the Semitic word itself and then its Greek equivalent, which is rendered “Christ.”

verse.text: And they asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered, “No.”
verse.note: The questions name figures expected at the end of the age. Elijah was to return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5), and “the Prophet” is the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18. The word is capitalized here to show that a specific expected figure is meant.

verse.text: So they said to him, “Who are you? We must give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”
He said, “I am a voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as the prophet Isaiah said.”
Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.

note.term: they had been sent from the Pharisees
note.traditional: they which were sent were of the Pharisees

verse.note: The Greek can mean that the delegation had been sent by the Pharisees, that the delegates themselves belonged to the Pharisees, or that some Pharisees had also been sent. The rendering here leaves the first two possibilities open.

verse.text: They questioned him and said to him, “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Messiah, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?”
John answered them, “I baptize with water. Among you stands one you do not know,

text.q: the one coming after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie.”

verse.text: These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!

text.q: This is the one about whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who has come to be ahead of me, because he was before me.’
I myself did not know him, but I came baptizing with water for this reason: that he might be revealed to Israel.”

verse.text: And John testified, “I have seen the Spirit coming down like a dove from heaven, and it stayed on him.

text.q: I myself did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize with water said to me, ‘The one on whom you see the Spirit coming down and staying—this is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’
And I have seen, and I have testified that this is the Chosen One of God.”

verse.note: The great majority of manuscripts, including very early ones, read “the Son of God,” and most translations follow them. A small number of early witnesses, including the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus, read “the Chosen One of God.” The Greek edition translated here adopts that reading on the ground that scribes were more likely to change it to the familiar title than the reverse. The question remains disputed.

verse.text: The next day John was again standing there with two of his disciples,
and looking at Jesus as he walked by, he said, “Look, the Lamb of God!”
The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.
Jesus turned and saw them following, and said to them, “What are you looking for?” They said to him, “Rabbi” (which, translated, means Teacher), “where are you staying?”
He said to them, “Come, and you will see.” So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the tenth hour is about four in the afternoon. A minority of scholars have argued that John counts from midnight, which would make it ten in the morning.

verse.text: Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard John and followed Jesus.
He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah” (which, translated, is Christ).
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon, son of John. You will be called Cephas” (which is translated Peter).
verse.note: Cephas represents the Aramaic word for “rock,” and Peter is the Greek equivalent. Neither seems to have been a usual personal name at the time, so a first-century hearer would have heard a nickname meaning something like “Rock.”

verse.text: The next day he decided to leave for Galilee. He found Philip, and Jesus said to him, “Follow me.”
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael and said to him, “We have found the one Moses wrote about in the Law, and the prophets also wrote about—Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth.”
Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”
Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, “Look, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit!”
Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, while you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”
Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”
Jesus answered him, “Do you believe because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.”
And he said to him, “Truly, truly, I tell you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

note.term: ascending and descending on the Son of Man

verse.note: Although Jesus is speaking to Nathanael, “you” is plural in Greek in this verse, so the promise extends to the other disciples. The image recalls Jacob’s dream in Genesis 28:12 of a stairway between earth and heaven with God’s angels ascending and descending on it; here the Son of Man takes the place of the stairway.

verse.text: On the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.
Jesus too was invited to the wedding, along with his disciples.
When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”
And Jesus said to her, “Woman, what is this to me and to you? My hour has not yet come.”

note.term: what is this to me and to you
note.traditional: what have I to do with thee? / what does this have to do with me?

verse.note: The Greek is a set idiom, literally “What to me and to you?”, familiar from the Septuagint. It usually means “What business do we have with each other?” and can range from a hostile rebuff to a mild refusal to be drawn in. Some take it here as “What concern is that of ours?”, others as “Why do you involve me?” Either way Jesus distances himself from the request, and the next sentence gives his reason.

In Greek this was a normal and courteous way to address a woman, without the brusqueness “Woman” has in modern English. It is nevertheless an unusual way for a son to address his mother. Jesus uses it for her again from the cross (19:26).

verse.text: His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”
Now six stone water jars were standing there, for the purification rites of the Jews, each holding two or three measures.

note.traditional: two or three firkins / twenty or thirty gallons

verse.note: The measure named here was a standard liquid unit of roughly ten gallons (about thirty-nine liters). Each jar therefore held some twenty to thirty gallons, and the six together well over a hundred. Stone vessels were favored for purification water because stone was held not to contract ritual impurity.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them to the brim.
Then he said to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet.” So they took it.

note.traditional: governor of the feast / master of the feast

verse.note: The word is rare and denotes the person in charge of a dinner. It is not certain whether this was a head servant who managed the food and wine or a guest chosen to preside over the feast. His easy manner with the bridegroom in verse 10 may favor the second.

verse.text: When the master of the banquet tasted the water that had become wine—he did not know where it came from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew—the master of the banquet called the bridegroom
and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and then the poorer wine once people are drunk. You have kept the good wine until now.”

note.traditional: when men have well drunk / when people have drunk freely

verse.note: The verb means to become drunk, and many versions soften it. The speaker is quoting a general rule of hospitality with some humor; the remark does not say that the guests at this wedding were drunk.

verse.text: Jesus did this, the first of his signs, in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory, and his disciples put their trust in him.
verse.note: The verb covers both “believe” and “trust”. “Trust” is used here and in verse 23, where John has the construction “believe into” a person, so that the wordplay in verses 23–24 can be heard: many trusted in Jesus, but he did not entrust himself to them, using the same verb. In verse 22, where the object is the Scripture and Jesus’s word, the same verb is rendered “believed”.

verse.text: After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there a few days.
The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
In the temple he found those selling cattle, sheep, and doves, and the money changers sitting there.
Making a whip out of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, both the sheep and the cattle; he poured out the money changers’ coins and overturned their tables,

note.term: drove them all out of the temple, both the sheep and the cattle
note.traditional: drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen

verse.note: The Greek can mean that Jesus drove out all the sellers together with their animals, or that “all” refers to the animals, “both the sheep and the cattle”. The grammar allows either, and scholars are divided. The rendering here follows the second reading while leaving the first possible.

verse.text: and to those selling the doves he said, “Take these away from here! Stop making my Father’s house a house of trade.”
His disciples remembered that it is written: “Zeal for your house will consume me.”

note.term: Zeal for your house will consume me.

verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 69:9 (68:10 in the Greek numbering), a psalm of a righteous sufferer that early Christians often applied to Jesus. The psalm speaks of zeal that “has consumed” the speaker; John’s future tense, “will consume”, points ahead to Jesus’s death.

verse.text: So the Jews responded and said to him, “What sign can you show us for doing these things?”
verse.note: John often uses this term for the Jerusalem authorities and not for the Jewish people as a whole, and those who challenge Jesus’s right to act in the temple may well be its officials. Some versions therefore render “the Jewish leaders” here. The text does not identify them further, so the general term is kept. Jesus and his disciples were, of course, Jews themselves.

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Destroy this sanctuary, and in three days I will raise it.”
verse.note: Greek has two words that most English versions both render “temple”. The word in verses 14–15 names the whole complex with its courts, where the traders were. The word here names the sanctuary building itself, the dwelling place of God, which suits its application to Jesus’s body in verse 21. Scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers keep the two apart, and verse 20 is often cited as a looser use. “Raise” is the same verb used for Jesus’s resurrection in verse 22.

verse.text: The Jews then said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this sanctuary, and you are going to raise it in three days?”

note.term: It has taken forty-six years to build this sanctuary
note.traditional: Forty and six years was this temple in building

verse.note: The Greek can mean that the building was completed over forty-six years or that it has been under construction for forty-six years so far. Herod the Great began rebuilding about 20–19 BC, and work on the complex continued until the 60s AD, so the second sense fits the history. Counting forty-six years from the start places this scene around AD 27–28.

verse.text: But he was speaking about the sanctuary of his body.
So when he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
While he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the festival, many put their trust in his name, seeing the signs he was doing.
But Jesus, for his part, would not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people
and had no need for anyone to testify about a person, for he himself knew what was in a person.
Now there was a man from among the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a leader of the Jews.
He came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.”
Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born from above, they cannot see the kingdom of God.”
verse.note: The Greek word can mean either “from above” or “again,” and the dialogue plays on both: Nicodemus hears “a second time” (verse 4), while Jesus goes on to speak of birth from the Spirit. Elsewhere in John, including verse 31 of this chapter, the word always means “from above,” so that sense is given here. Many translations keep “born again,” and scholars widely agree that the double meaning is deliberate.

verse.text: Nicodemus said to him, “How can a person be born when already old? Surely no one can enter their mother’s womb a second time and be born?”
Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born of water and Spirit, they cannot enter the kingdom of God.

text.q: What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Do not be amazed that I told you, ‘You must be born from above.’

note.term: You must be born from above

verse.note: The “you” inside this quotation is plural in Greek, as it is in “you do not accept” (verse 11) and throughout verse 12. Jesus is addressing Nicodemus as the representative of a group, just as Nicodemus began with “we know” in verse 2.

text.q: The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

verse.note: The same Greek word means “wind,” “breath,” and “spirit,” and it is the word translated “Spirit” in verses 5, 6, and at the end of this verse. Likewise the word for the wind’s “sound” also means “voice.” The comparison is therefore a wordplay that English cannot reproduce: the Spirit, like the wind, is known by its effects and not by its origin or destination.

verse.text: Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things happen?”
Jesus answered him, “You are the teacher of Israel, and you do not understand these things?

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know and testify to what we have seen, yet you do not accept our testimony.
If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?
And no one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man.

note.traditional: the Son of man which is in heaven

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add “who is in heaven” after “the Son of Man,” and the King James Version includes it. The earliest surviving manuscripts lack the phrase, and the Greek text translated here omits it, though some scholars defend it as original.

text.q: And just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,

verse.note: The allusion is to Numbers 21:4–9, where Moses set a bronze snake on a pole and those bitten by snakes looked at it and lived. The verb also means “exalt,” and John uses it with both senses at once (see 8:28; 12:32–34): Jesus’ being raised on the cross is at the same time his exaltation.

text.q: so that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him.”

verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for “age.” In Jewish usage of the period “eternal life” meant the life of the age to come, so it describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. In John this life is something the believer already has (verse 36).

The phrase “in him” can be attached either to “believes” or to “have eternal life.” John normally writes “believe in” with a different preposition (as in verse 16), so here the phrase is taken with “have eternal life.” Many translations read “everyone who believes in him may have eternal life,” and some manuscripts have the wording that favors that reading.

verse.text: For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.

note.term: For God so loved the world

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no quotation marks, and it is disputed where Jesus’ words to Nicodemus end. This translation closes the speech at verse 15 and treats verses 16–21 as the evangelist’s reflection, because the language shifts to the past tense and to terms characteristic of the narrator, such as “one and only Son.” Many translations and scholars instead continue Jesus’ speech through verse 21.

The Greek word means “only one of its kind” and was the ordinary term for an only child; its second element comes from the word for “kind,” not the verb “beget.” “One and only” or “only” is the rendering of most modern translations, though a minority of scholars have recently defended “only begotten.”

verse.text: For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.
verse.note: Most English versions render the verb “condemn” in verses 17–18 and then switch to “judgment” or “verdict” for the related noun in verse 19. The Greek uses one word family throughout, and “judge” and “judgment” keep that link visible. The context makes clear that an unfavorable judgment is meant, which is why “condemn” is the common choice.

verse.text: Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has been judged already, because they have not believed in the name of the one and only Son of God.
And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light, because their deeds were evil.
For everyone who does what is base hates the light and does not come to the light, so that their deeds may not be exposed.
But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that their deeds may be shown to have been done in God.
After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and there he spent time with them and was baptizing.
John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was plenty of water there, and people were coming and being baptized;
for John had not yet been thrown into prison.
Then a dispute arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew about purification.
They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you have testified—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him.”
John answered, “No one can receive even one thing unless it has been given to them from heaven.

text.q: You yourselves testify for me that I said, ‘I am not the Messiah,’ but, ‘I have been sent ahead of him.’

verse.note: The Greek word, traditionally “Christ,” translates the Hebrew title “Messiah,” the anointed king Israel expected. Here John is denying a title, not a name, so “Messiah” is used. Several modern translations make the same distinction, using “Messiah” where the title is under discussion in the Gospels and “Christ” elsewhere.

text.q: The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the bridegroom’s friend, who stands and listens to him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. So this joy of mine is now complete.
He must increase, and I must decrease.”

verse.text: The one who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth. The one who comes from heaven is above all.

note.term: The one who comes from above

verse.note: As with verse 16, it is uncertain who is speaking in verses 31–36. This translation ends John the Baptist’s words at verse 30 and takes the rest as the evangelist’s comment, since the passage echoes the language of verses 11–18. Some translations and scholars treat it as the continuation of John’s speech.

verse.text: He testifies to what he has seen and heard, yet no one accepts his testimony.
Whoever has accepted his testimony has set their seal to this, that God is true.
For the one whom God sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.

note.term: he gives the Spirit without measure
note.traditional: God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him

verse.note: The Greek does not state who gives or who receives. Most interpreters understand that God gives the Spirit without limit to the one he sent, and some manuscripts and translations make this explicit by adding “God” or “to him.” It is also possible to read the one sent as the giver of the Spirit.

verse.text: The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever disobeys the Son will not see life; rather, the wrath of God remains on them.
Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—
verse.note: The Greek text followed here reads “Jesus”; many manuscripts, including some early ones, read “the Lord” instead. Editors are divided over which is original. The meaning of the sentence is unaffected.

verse.text: though Jesus himself was not baptizing; his disciples were—
he left Judea and set off again for Galilee.
He had to pass through Samaria.
So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of land that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.
Jacob’s spring was there. So Jesus, tired from the journey, sat down just as he was by the spring. It was about the sixth hour.
verse.note: The Greek word here and in verse 14 means a spring or source of flowing water. The woman in verses 11–12 uses a different word that means a dug well. Most translations have “well” throughout, but keeping the two words apart shows that Jesus’s “spring of water” in verse 14 picks up the narrator’s word, not the woman’s.

Hours were normally counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon, the hottest part of the day. A minority of scholars think John counts from midnight or noon, which would make it about six in the evening; most do not. The “seventh hour” in verse 52 is, on the usual reckoning, about one in the afternoon.

verse.text: A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”
For his disciples had gone off into the town to buy food.
So the Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.
verse.note: The verb can mean to associate with someone, which is the traditional reading. It can also mean to use something together with someone, in which case the point is that Jews would not share a drinking vessel with Samaritans for reasons of purity. Scholars are divided, and the second reading suits the scene well. The sentence is the narrator’s aside and is absent from a few early manuscripts.

verse.text: Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”
verse.note: “Living water” was the ordinary expression for fresh, flowing water from a spring or stream, as opposed to still water in a cistern. The woman takes it in that everyday sense, which is why she asks where he will get it. Jesus means water that gives life, and in the Scriptures God himself is called a fountain of living water.

verse.text: The woman said to him, “Sir, you have no bucket, and the well is deep. So where do you get this living water?

text.q: Surely you are not greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, along with his sons and his livestock?”

verse.text: Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again,

text.q: but whoever drinks of the water that I will give them will never be thirsty. Rather, the water that I will give them will become in them a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”

verse.text: The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to keep coming all the way here to draw.”
He said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come back here.”
The woman answered him, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right to say, ‘I have no husband,’

text.q: for you have had five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband. In this you have spoken the truth.”

verse.text: The woman said to him, “Sir, I see that you are a prophet.

text.q: Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you people say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.”

verse.note: The mountain is Gerizim, which rises above the site of the conversation. Samaritans held that it, not Jerusalem, was the place God had chosen for worship. A Samaritan temple had stood there until the Judean ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed it in the late second century BC.

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “Believe me, woman, an hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.

text.q: You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews.
But an hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for indeed the Father is seeking such people to worship him.

verse.note: Greek manuscripts do not distinguish capital letters, so “spirit” here could be the human spirit, or a spiritual mode of worship, or God’s own Spirit. The lowercase matches “God is spirit” in verse 24. Many interpreters think John means worship made possible by the Spirit that Jesus gives, and that “spirit and truth” form a single idea.

text.q: God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”

verse.text: The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming, the one called Christ. When he comes, he will tell us everything.”
verse.note: “Messiah” is a Semitic word meaning “anointed one” and “Christ” is its Greek translation. The explanation is probably the evangelist’s gloss for Greek readers, as at 1:41, though the Greek does not mark it off from the woman’s words. “Christ” is kept here because the verse is giving the Greek equivalent of the term.

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one speaking to you.”

note.traditional: I that speak unto thee am he

verse.note: The Greek is simply “I am, the one speaking to you.” In context it means “I am he,” that is, the Messiah she has just mentioned. The same two words are used for God’s self-declaration in the Greek version of Isaiah and are used pointedly by Jesus later in John (8:58). Many scholars hear that overtone here; others take it as plain self-identification.

verse.text: Just then his disciples came, and they were amazed that he was talking with a woman. Yet no one said, “What do you want?” or “Why are you talking with her?”
So the woman left her water jar, went off into the town, and said to the people,

text.q: “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did! Could this be the Messiah?”

verse.note: The Greek is “the Christ,” used here as a title for the expected anointed figure and not as a name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader, and several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. The form of the woman’s question in Greek is tentative; it does not assert that he is.

verse.text: They went out of the town and were making their way to him.
Meanwhile the disciples kept urging him, “Rabbi, eat.”
But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you do not know about.”
So the disciples said to one another, “Surely no one has brought him something to eat?”
Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of the one who sent me and to complete his work.

text.q: Do you not say, ‘Four months more, and then the harvest comes’? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes and see the fields: they are white for harvest. Already

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, so “already” can end this sentence (“white for harvest already”) or begin the next (“Already the reaper is receiving wages”). The Greek edition followed here takes it with what follows, though the word stands at the end of verse 35. Both readings have support among translators and commentators.

text.q: the reaper is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together.
For in this the saying is true: ‘One sows and another reaps.’
I sent you to reap what you have not labored for. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”

verse.text: Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified, “He told me everything I did.”
So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.
And many more believed because of his word,
and they said to the woman, “We no longer believe because of what you said, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this truly is the Savior of the world.”
After the two days he left there for Galilee,
for Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own homeland.
verse.note: It is disputed which place John means. In the other Gospels the saying refers to Nazareth in Galilee, but here the Galileans welcome Jesus in the next verse. For that reason some take the homeland to be Judea or Jerusalem, which he has just left. Others think the Galilean welcome, based only on signs, is itself the lack of honor.

verse.text: So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the festival, for they too had gone to the festival.
So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had turned the water into wine. Now there was a certain royal official whose son was sick in Capernaum.
When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for the boy was about to die.
So Jesus said to him, “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will never believe.”
The royal official said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”
Jesus said to him, “Go; your son lives.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and set off.
While he was still on his way down, his slaves met him and told him that his boy was alive.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes people who were owned, not hired staff. “Servants” is the traditional English, and it softens this. A royal official’s household would ordinarily have included slaves.

verse.text: So he asked them the hour at which the boy had begun to get better, and they told him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.”
So the father realized that it was at that very hour that Jesus had said to him, “Your son lives.” And he himself believed, and his whole household.
This was now the second sign that Jesus did, after he had come from Judea to Galilee.
After this there was a festival of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
Now there is in Jerusalem, by the Sheep Gate, a pool called in Hebrew Bethesda, which has five colonnades.
verse.note: The Greek has only an adjective, “the sheep-related,” with no noun. Most translations supply “gate,” after the Sheep Gate of Nehemiah 3:1 on the north side of the temple area. Some instead read “by the Sheep Pool there is a place called Bethesda,” and the oldest translations took it that way.

The Greek word means “in the language of the Hebrews” and does not distinguish Hebrew from Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in Judea at the time. Several of the names John labels this way are Aramaic in form, so some translations render “in Aramaic.”
The manuscripts give the name in several forms, chiefly Bethesda, Bethzatha and Bethsaida. SBLGNT reads Bethesda; some other critical editions prefer Bethzatha. The original form is uncertain.

verse.text: In these lay a crowd of the sick—blind, lame, paralyzed.

note.traditional: blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts lack the end of verse 3 and all of verse 4, which is why the numbering passes from 3 to 5. Later manuscripts add that the sick were waiting for the water to move, because an angel came down from time to time and stirred the pool, and the first to step in afterward was healed. Most scholars regard this as an early explanation of verse 7 that entered the text from the margin.

verse.text: One man was there who had been ill for thirty-eight years.
When Jesus saw him lying there and learned that he had already been in that condition a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to become well?”
The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up; and while I am on my way, someone else goes down ahead of me.”
Jesus said to him, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.”
And at once the man became well, and he picked up his mat and began to walk. Now that day was a Sabbath.
So the Jewish leaders said to the man who had been healed, “It is the Sabbath, and you are not permitted to carry your mat.”
verse.note: The Greek says simply “the Jews,” as in verse 1. Here and through verse 18 the group in view is the authorities in Jerusalem who police Sabbath observance, not the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus, the healed man and the crowd are all Jews. Scholars are divided on how to render John’s usage, some preferring “Judeans” throughout and others keeping “the Jews” everywhere.

note.term: you are not permitted to carry your mat

verse.note: Carrying a load on the Sabbath was understood to be forbidden work (compare Jeremiah 17:21–22), and later rabbinic law lists carrying an object from one place to another among the prohibited kinds of labor. The objection is to the carrying, not to the healing as such, though verse 16 extends the charge to Jesus.

verse.text: But he answered them, “The man who made me well—he told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’”
They asked him, “Who is the man who told you, ‘Pick it up and walk’?”
But the man who had been cured did not know who it was, for Jesus had slipped away, as there was a crowd in the place.
Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, “See, you have become well. Sin no longer, so that nothing worse happens to you.”
The man went away and told the Jewish leaders that it was Jesus who had made him well.
And for this reason the Jewish leaders began to persecute Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.
But he answered them, “My Father is working even until now, and I too am working.”

note.term: My Father is working even until now

verse.note: Genesis says God rested on the seventh day, but Jewish interpreters of the period commonly held that God never stops sustaining the world, giving life and judging, even on the Sabbath. Jesus claims the same exemption for himself, which is why verse 18 treats the saying as a claim to equality with God.

verse.text: For this reason, then, the Jewish leaders sought all the more to kill him, because he was not only breaking the Sabbath but was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God.
So Jesus answered and said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing on his own, only what he sees the Father doing; for whatever the Father does, the Son also does in the same way.

text.q: For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself is doing, and he will show him greater works than these, so that you will be amazed.
For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those he wishes.
Nor does the Father judge anyone; he has given all judgment to the Son,
so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears my word and believes the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has crossed over from death to life.

verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for “age.” In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length. John stresses that the believer has it already.

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.
For just as the Father has life in himself, so also he has granted the Son to have life in himself;
and he has given him authority to carry out judgment, because he is the Son of Man.

verse.note: Only here in the Gospels does the phrase lack the Greek definite articles, so it could mean “a son of man,” that is, a human being: authority to judge is given him because he is human. Most interpreters take it as the title, noting that the Greek of Daniel 7:13, where “one like a son of man” receives authority, also lacks the article.

text.q: Do not be amazed at this, for an hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice
and will come out—those who have done good, to a resurrection of life, and those who have practiced evil, to a resurrection of judgment.
I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will but the will of the one who sent me.
If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true.

verse.note: The language is that of a courtroom. Under the Law a matter had to be established by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and a person’s unsupported testimony on his own behalf did not count. “Not true” here means not admissible as valid evidence, not that it is false; Jesus goes on to name his other witnesses.

text.q: There is another who testifies about me, and I know that the testimony he gives about me is true.
You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth.
I, however, do not accept testimony from a human being; but I say these things so that you may be saved.
He was the lamp, burning and shining, and you were willing for a while to rejoice in his light.
But I have a testimony greater than John’s: the works that the Father has given me to complete—the very works I am doing—testify about me that the Father has sent me.
And the Father who sent me has himself testified about me. You have never heard his voice or seen his form,
and you do not have his word remaining in you, because you do not believe the one he sent.
You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that testify about me,

verse.note: The Greek verb form can be either a statement (“You search”) or a command (“Search”). Older translations took it as a command. Most modern translations and commentators read a statement, since the following words explain why the hearers already do this and the point is that they miss what the Scriptures say.

text.q: yet you are unwilling to come to me so that you may have life.
I do not accept glory from people,
but I know you: you do not have the love of God within you.

verse.note: The phrase can mean love for God or the love that comes from God. Most interpreters take it here as love for God, which the hearers lack despite their devotion to the Scriptures. The translation keeps the ambiguity of the Greek.

text.q: I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not accept me; if another comes in his own name, you will accept him.
How can you believe, when you accept glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?
Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope.
For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.
But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”

verse.text: After this Jesus went away across the Sea of Galilee, the Sea of Tiberias.
A large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs he was performing on the sick.
Jesus went up the mountain, and there he sat with his disciples.
Now the Passover, the festival of the Jews, was near.
So when Jesus looked up and saw that a large crowd was coming toward him, he said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread so that these people may eat?”
He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do.
Philip answered him, “Bread worth two hundred denarii would not be enough for each of them to get a little.”
verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a laborer. Two hundred denarii was therefore well over half a year’s wages.

verse.text: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,

text.q: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish—but what are these among so many?”

verse.text: Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was plenty of grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.
Then Jesus took the loaves, and after giving thanks he distributed them to those who were seated, and likewise of the fish, as much as they wanted.
When they were satisfied, he said to his disciples, “Gather up the leftover pieces, so that nothing is lost.”
So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with pieces from the five barley loaves, left over by those who had eaten.
When the people saw the sign he had performed, they began to say, “This truly is the Prophet who is to come into the world.”
verse.note: Many Jews expected a prophet like Moses, promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18. A miraculous feeding in a remote place near Passover would have recalled Moses and the manna, which explains both this reaction and the attempt to make Jesus king in the next verse.

verse.text: So Jesus, knowing that they were about to come and seize him to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself, alone.
When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,
got into a boat, and set out across the sea for Capernaum. Darkness had already fallen, and Jesus had not yet come to them,
and the sea was being stirred up because a strong wind was blowing.
When they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were afraid.
verse.note: A stadion was about 185 meters, so the distance is roughly three to three and a half miles (five to six kilometers). That places the boat far out from shore.

verse.text: But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally “I am,” the ordinary way of saying “It’s me.” In the Greek Old Testament the same words also serve as God’s self-declaration, and John has Jesus use them that way elsewhere (8:58). Many scholars hear that overtone here, in a scene of mastery over the sea; others take it as simple self-identification.

verse.text: Then they wanted to take him into the boat, and at once the boat reached the land they were heading for.

The next day the crowd that had stayed on the other side of the sea saw that there had been no other small boat there except one, and that Jesus had not gotten into the boat with his disciples, but his disciples had gone away alone.
But small boats came from Tiberias, near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the small boats and went to Capernaum, looking for Jesus.
When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, “Rabbi, when did you get here?”
Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, you are looking for me not because you saw signs but because you ate of the loaves and had your fill.

text.q: Do not work for the food that perishes but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you. For on him God the Father has set his seal.”

verse.note: In Jewish usage of the period, “eternal life” is the life of the age to come. The word describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. In John the believer already has this life (verse 47), though resurrection “on the last day” is still to come.

verse.text: So they said to him, “What are we to do, so that we may work the works of God?”
Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God: that you believe in the one he sent.”
So they said to him, “Then what sign are you going to perform, so that we may see it and believe you? What work are you doing?

text.q: Our ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written, ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”

note.term: He gave them bread from heaven to eat

verse.note: The quotation is closest to Psalm 78:24 and recalls the manna story of Exodus 16. The crowd is asking Jesus to match Moses. The grumbling in verses 41 and 61 uses the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel’s complaints in the wilderness.

verse.text: So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, it is not Moses who has given you the bread from heaven; rather, my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.

text.q: For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”

note.term: that which comes down from heaven
note.traditional: he who comes down from heaven

verse.note: The Greek can mean either “that which comes down” (the bread) or “he who comes down” (a person), because “bread” is grammatically masculine. The crowd’s reply in verse 34 shows they heard it of bread; verse 35 reveals that Jesus means himself. Translations are divided, and the double meaning is probably intended.

verse.text: So they said to him, “Sir, give us this bread always.”
Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never go hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.

text.q: But I told you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.
All that the Father gives me will come to me, and the one who comes to me I will never throw out,
because I have come down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of the one who sent me.
And this is the will of the one who sent me: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.
For this is the will of my Father: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day.”

verse.text: So the Jews began grumbling about him because he had said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven,”
and they were saying, “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How can he now say, ‘I have come down from heaven’?”
Jesus answered them, “Stop grumbling among yourselves.

text.q: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws them, and I will raise them up on the last day.
It is written in the Prophets, ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.
Not that anyone has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes has eternal life.
I am the bread of life.
Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.
This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die.
I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, they will live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world.”

verse.text: So the Jews began quarreling with one another, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”
So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves.

text.q: Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day.

verse.note: From here to verse 58 John switches to a different Greek verb for eating, one that in older Greek meant to gnaw or munch. Some interpreters see a deliberately more physical word and render it “feeds on” or “chews.” Many lexicographers hold that by this period it had become an everyday present-tense word for “eat,” so it is rendered “eats” here.

text.q: For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.
Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in them.
Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me.
This is the bread that came down from heaven. It is not like what the ancestors ate, and died; whoever eats this bread will live forever.”

verse.text: He said these things in the synagogue as he was teaching in Capernaum.
When they heard this, many of his disciples said, “This saying is harsh; who can listen to it?”
verse.note: “Hard” in modern English suggests “difficult to understand.” The Greek word means hard in the sense of harsh, rough or offensive. The disciples are complaining that the saying is intolerable, not that it is obscure.

verse.text: But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Does this cause you to stumble?
verse.note: The verb means to trip someone up so that they fall in their loyalty to God. “Offend” now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak for a saying that makes many disciples leave (verse 66). Modern versions are divided here between “offend” and “cause to stumble.”

text.q: Then what if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?
The Spirit is the one who gives life; the flesh is of no use at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and are life.

note.traditional: It is the Spirit who gives life

verse.note: Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so “spirit” here could be God’s Spirit or spirit as opposed to flesh. Most translations capitalize the first occurrence and leave the second (“are spirit and are life”) in lowercase, as here, but the line between the two is not sharp in John.

verse.text: But there are some of you who do not believe.” For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was that would hand him over.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing a person into someone else’s custody. The Gospels use the same word for what Judas, the chief priests and Pilate each do to Jesus. Most versions render it “betray” when Judas is the subject, which fits the context but hides that chain. Some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual sense.

verse.text: And he said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted to them by the Father.”
At this, many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.
So Jesus said to the Twelve, “You do not want to go away too, do you?”
Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life,

text.q: and we have come to believe and to know that you are the Holy One of God.”

note.traditional: that Christ, the Son of the living God

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “the Christ, the Son of the living God.” The earliest witnesses have the shorter “the Holy One of God.” The longer form is generally judged to have been adapted to Peter’s confession in Matthew 16:16.

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil.”
He was speaking of Judas son of Simon Iscariot, for this man, one of the Twelve, was going to hand him over.
After this Jesus went about in Galilee, for he did not want to go about in Judea, because the Judeans were seeking to kill him.
verse.note: The Greek word names a people with a religion and a homeland, and no single English word covers it. Here the contrast is geographic, Judea as against Galilee, so “Judeans” is used. In verses 11 and 13, where the group is distinguished from the festival crowds and is feared by them, it is rendered “the Jewish leaders”; elsewhere in the chapter it is “the Jews.” Scholars are divided: some prefer “Judeans” throughout, while others object that this erases Jews from the New Testament.

verse.text: Now the festival of the Jews, the Festival of Booths, was near.
verse.note: This was the week-long autumn harvest festival, one of the three pilgrimage festivals, during which people lived in temporary shelters recalling Israel’s years in the wilderness (Leviticus 23:33–43). Later Jewish sources describe a daily water-pouring ceremony at the temple during the festival, which many scholars see as the setting for Jesus’ words about thirst and living water in verses 37–38.

verse.text: So his brothers said to him, “Leave here and go to Judea, so that your disciples too may see the works you are doing.

text.q: For no one does anything in secret while seeking to be in the public eye himself. If you are doing these things, show yourself to the world.”

verse.text: For not even his brothers believed in him.
So Jesus said to them, “My time is not yet here, but your time is always at hand.

text.q: The world cannot hate you, but it hates me, because I testify about it that its works are evil.
You go up to the festival. I am not going up to this festival, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.”

verse.note: Some early and important manuscripts read “I am not yet going up,” which removes the apparent conflict with verse 10, where Jesus does go. Many editors, including those of the Greek text translated here, judge “not” to be the earlier reading, since a copyist would more likely ease the difficulty than create it. The question remains disputed.

verse.text: Having said this, he himself stayed in Galilee.
But when his brothers had gone up to the festival, then he too went up, not openly but, as it were, in secret.
So the Jewish leaders were looking for him at the festival and saying, “Where is that man?”
And there was much murmuring about him among the crowds. Some were saying, “He is a good man,” but others were saying, “No, he is leading the crowd astray.”
Yet no one spoke publicly about him, for fear of the Jewish leaders.
When the festival was already half over, Jesus went up into the temple and began to teach.
So the Jews were amazed and said, “How does this man have such learning, when he has never studied?”
verse.note: The Greek says literally that he “knows letters.” The point is not basic literacy but trained learning, here in the Scriptures and their interpretation. Such learning was normally acquired by studying under a recognized teacher, which Jesus had not done.

verse.text: So Jesus answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but belongs to the one who sent me.

text.q: If anyone wants to do his will, that person will know about the teaching, whether it is from God or whether I speak on my own.
The one who speaks on his own seeks his own glory, but the one who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true, and there is no wrongdoing in him.
Has not Moses given you the Law? Yet none of you keeps the Law. Why are you seeking to kill me?”

verse.text: The crowd answered, “You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?”
Jesus answered them, “I did one work, and you are all amazed.

text.q: For this reason Moses has given you circumcision—not that it is from Moses, but from the patriarchs—and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath.

note.traditional: Moses therefore gave unto you circumcision

verse.note: The Greek phrase can be attached to the end of verse 21 (“you are all amazed because of it”) or, as here and in the Greek edition followed, to the beginning of verse 22. Taken with verse 22, the thought is compressed: Moses gave circumcision, which overrides the Sabbath, and this sets the precedent for the healing Jesus goes on to defend.

text.q: If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the Law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because I made a whole man well on the Sabbath?
Do not judge by appearance, but judge with just judgment.”

verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice.” Because fair judging is the point here, “just” is used; the same Greek adjective is elsewhere rendered “righteous.”

verse.text: So some of the people of Jerusalem were saying, “Is this not the man they are seeking to kill?

text.q: And look, he is speaking publicly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers have really recognized that this man is the Messiah?

verse.note: The Greek word means the anointed king Israel expected, and in this chapter it is a title under debate, not a name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader where “Christ” tends to sound like a surname. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it functions as a name.

text.q: But we know where this man is from; when the Messiah comes, no one knows where he is from.”

note.term: no one knows where he is from

verse.note: One strand of Jewish expectation held that the Messiah would appear suddenly, his origins hidden until he was revealed. Others in the crowd hold a different expectation in verse 42, that he must come from Bethlehem. John lets both objections stand without comment, and Jesus answers by pointing to the one who sent him.

verse.text: So Jesus cried out as he was teaching in the temple, “You know me, and you know where I am from. Yet I have not come on my own; the one who sent me is true, and him you do not know.

text.q: I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.”

verse.text: So they were seeking to seize him, yet no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.
But many from the crowd believed in him, and they were saying, “When the Messiah comes, surely he will not do more signs than this man has done?”
The Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring these things about him, and the chief priests and the Pharisees sent officers to seize him.
So Jesus said, “I am with you a little while longer, and then I am going to the one who sent me.

text.q: You will look for me and will not find me, and where I am, you cannot come.”

verse.text: So the Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go, that we will not find him? Surely he does not intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks?
verse.note: “The Dispersion” was the standard term for Jews living scattered outside the land of Israel, here those in Greek-speaking regions. “Greeks” in the second clause most likely means non-Jews. The speakers intend the suggestion as absurd.

text.q: What is this saying of his, ‘You will look for me and will not find me, and where I am, you cannot come’?”

verse.text: On the last day of the festival, the great day, Jesus stood and cried out, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink.

text.q: Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Rivers of living water will flow from within him.’”

verse.note: The punctuation is disputed. The text follows the usual division, in which the rivers flow from within the believer. The words can also be divided as “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me, and let whoever believes in me drink,” in which case the Scripture may describe the water flowing from Jesus himself. No single Old Testament passage matches the quotation; passages such as Isaiah 58:11, Ezekiel 47:1–12 and Zechariah 14:8 are often suggested.

The Greek word means the belly or the womb, and it was also used for a person’s inner self. Older versions have “belly” and several modern ones “heart”; “from within him” gives the sense without suggesting anatomy that the saying does not intend.

verse.text: Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive; for as yet there was no Spirit, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

note.term: as yet there was no Spirit
note.traditional: the Spirit had not yet been given

verse.note: The Greek says simply that the Spirit “was not yet.” Some manuscripts add “given,” and most translations supply it. John is not saying that the Spirit did not exist (compare 1:32–33); he means that the Spirit was not yet present with believers in the way that would follow once Jesus was glorified.

verse.text: So some from the crowd, when they heard these words, were saying, “This truly is the Prophet.”
verse.note: With the definite article this refers to a particular expected figure, the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18. The crowd treats this figure as distinct from the Messiah, as in 1:20–21.

verse.text: Others were saying, “This is the Messiah.” But some were saying, “Surely the Messiah does not come from Galilee?

text.q: Has not the Scripture said that the Messiah comes from the offspring of David, and from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”

verse.text: So a division arose in the crowd because of him.
Some of them wanted to seize him, but no one laid hands on him.
So the officers came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, “Why did you not bring him?”
The officers answered, “Never has anyone spoken like this!”
So the Pharisees answered them, “Surely you have not been led astray too?

text.q: Has any of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees?
But this crowd that does not know the Law—they are accursed.”

verse.text: Nicodemus, who had come to him earlier and was one of them, said to them,

text.q: “Surely our Law does not judge a person without first hearing from him and learning what he is doing?”

verse.text: They answered him, “Surely you are not from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”
Then Jesus spoke to them again, saying, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”

note.term: Then Jesus spoke to them again

verse.note: Verses 1–11 of this chapter belong to the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11). That passage is missing from the earliest manuscripts and appears at different places in later ones, and most scholars judge that it was not originally part of this Gospel. Without it, verse 12 continues directly from the debate in the temple at the end of chapter 7.

The setting is still the Feast of Tabernacles (7:2, 37). Later rabbinic tradition describes great lamps lit in the temple’s Court of Women during that festival, the area where the treasury of verse 20 is usually located. Many interpreters hear the saying against that backdrop, though John does not mention the lamps.

verse.text: So the Pharisees said to him, “You are testifying about yourself; your testimony is not true.”
Jesus answered them, “Even if I do testify about myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going. But you do not know where I come from or where I am going.

text.q: You judge by human standards; I judge no one.

verse.note: The Greek is literally “according to the flesh.” Here “flesh” means the merely human point of view—judging by appearances and human criteria—not the body or sinful desire. Several modern versions render it the same way.

text.q: Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, because I am not alone—it is I and the Father who sent me.
And in your own Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true.

note.term: the testimony of two people is true

verse.note: The rule that a matter must be established by two or three witnesses comes from Deuteronomy 17:6 and 19:15. “True” here carries the legal sense “valid,” as in verses 13 and 14. Jesus names himself and the Father as the two witnesses.

text.q: I am the one who testifies about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me.”

verse.text: So they asked him, “Where is your father?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.”
He spoke these words in the treasury while teaching in the temple, and no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come.
Then he said to them again, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come.”
So the Jews said, “He is not going to kill himself, is he, since he says, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?”
He said to them, “You are from below; I am from above. You are from this world; I am not from this world.

text.q: That is why I told you that you will die in your sins; for unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.”

verse.note: The Greek is simply “I am” (egō eimi) with nothing after it, which is why the hearers ask “Who are you?” in the next verse. In everyday Greek the phrase can mean “I am he” or “it is I,” and it is rendered that way here and in verse 28; it also echoes God’s self-declaration in the Greek version of Isaiah (for example 43:10). The same two words stand in verse 58, where nothing can be supplied and the rendering is “I am.”

verse.text: So they said to him, “Who are you?” Jesus said to them, “Why do I speak to you at all?

note.term: Why do I speak to you at all?
note.traditional: Just what I have been telling you from the beginning

verse.note: This is one of the most disputed sentences in John. The traditional rendering takes the opening phrase as “from the beginning,” but used adverbially it often means “at all,” John elsewhere uses a different expression for “from the beginning,” and the verb is in the present tense. The Greek edition translated here punctuates the sentence as a question, and ancient Greek-speaking commentators read it as an expression of exasperation. Many scholars and most English versions still prefer the traditional sense.

text.q: I have much to say about you and much to judge, but the one who sent me is true, and what I have heard from him I speak to the world.”

verse.text: They did not understand that he was speaking to them about the Father.
So Jesus said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own, but speak these things just as the Father taught me.
verse.note: The verb means both to raise physically and to exalt. John uses it for Jesus being raised on the cross, which is at the same time his exaltation (3:14; 12:32–33). “Lifted up” keeps both senses.

text.q: And the one who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him.”

verse.text: As he was saying these things, many believed in him.
So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples,

note.term: the Jews who had believed him

verse.note: These hearers are said to have believed him, yet in the verses that follow the audience is said to be seeking to kill him. Some interpreters think their belief was shallow and gives way under challenge. Others think the group addressed widens again to the hostile crowd of the earlier verses. The text does not settle the question.

text.q: and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”

verse.text: They answered him, “We are Abraham’s descendants and have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will become free’?”
Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.

text.q: The slave does not remain in the household forever; the son remains forever.

note.term: does not remain in the household forever
note.traditional: does not remain in the house forever

verse.note: The Greek idiom, literally “into the age,” usually means “never” when it follows a negative, as in verses 51 and 52. Here the contrast with the son who “remains forever” shows that the sense is “not permanently” rather than “never”: a slave has no lasting place in the household, and a son does.

text.q: So if the Son sets you free, you will really be free.
I know that you are Abraham’s descendants. Yet you are seeking to kill me, because my word finds no room in you.
I speak what I have seen in my Father’s presence, and you, then, do what you have heard from your father.”

note.term: do what you have heard from your father
note.traditional: you do what you have heard from your father

verse.note: The Greek has simply “the father” in both halves of the verse, and the verb “do” can be a statement or a command. The rendering here takes it as a contrast between two fathers, anticipating verses 41 and 44, as most English versions do. The alternative is an appeal: “so you too should do what you have heard from the Father.” Some manuscripts add “my” and “your” to make the contrast explicit.

verse.text: They answered him, “Our father is Abraham.” Jesus said to them, “If you are Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works of Abraham.

text.q: But now you are seeking to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham did not do this.

verse.text: You are doing the works of your father.” They said to him, “We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father—God.”
verse.note: The word covers unlawful sexual relations in general. In the prophets it is also a standing image for idolatry—Hosea speaks of “children of whoredom”—which fits the reply “We have one Father—God”: the speakers claim to be faithful Israel, not children of a false god. Some interpreters also hear in the emphatic “We” a slur on the circumstances of Jesus’s own birth, but this is uncertain.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and am here. I have not come on my own; he sent me.

text.q: Why do you not understand what I am saying? Because you cannot hear my word.

You are from your father the devil, and you want to carry out your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar and the father of lies.

note.term: You are from your father the devil

verse.note: This is said within a dispute among Jews, to the particular hearers who, Jesus says, are seeking to kill him (verses 37 and 40). He has already granted that they are Abraham’s descendants; the argument is that conduct, not ancestry, shows whose child a person is. The verse was later turned against the Jewish people as a whole, a use the context does not support.

text.q: But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me.
Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?
Whoever is from God hears the words of God. This is why you do not hear: because you are not from God.”

verse.text: The Jews answered him, “Are we not right to say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?”
Jesus answered, “I do not have a demon. I honor my Father, and you dishonor me.

text.q: I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it, and he judges.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever keeps my word will never see death.”

verse.text: The Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and so did the prophets, yet you say, ‘Whoever keeps my word will never taste death.’

text.q: Surely you are not greater than our father Abraham, who died? The prophets died too. Who do you make yourself out to be?”

verse.text: Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, ‘He is our God.’

text.q: Yet you have not come to know him, but I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him, and I keep his word.
Your father Abraham was overjoyed that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

verse.text: So the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham?”
Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am.”
verse.note: These are the same two Greek words as in verses 24 and 28, here with nothing that could be supplied after them and set against Abraham’s coming into existence. Most interpreters hear an echo of God’s self-declarations in Isaiah, and many also connect it with the divine name in Exodus 3:14. The attempt at stoning in the next verse suggests the hearers took it as blasphemy.

verse.text: So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid and went out of the temple.
As he was passing by, he saw a man blind from birth.
His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but it was so that the works of God might be revealed in him.

note.traditional: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him

verse.note: The Greek has only “but so that,” with no verb, and most translations supply something like “this happened” or “it was.” A minority of interpreters punctuate differently, ending the sentence after “sinned” and attaching the clause to verse 4: “But so that the works of God may be revealed in him, we must do the works…” That reading avoids implying that the man was made blind for this purpose; the traditional punctuation is followed here as the majority view.

text.q: We must do the works of the one who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work.

note.term: We must do the works of the one who sent me
note.traditional: I must work the works of him that sent me

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “we must,” which draws the disciples into Jesus’s work; many later manuscripts read “I must,” the reading behind the King James Version. A few early witnesses also read “the one who sent us.” Most modern editions and translations adopt “we … sent me,” as here.

text.q: While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”
