verse.text: Having said this, he spat on the ground and made mud with the saliva, and he smeared the mud on the man’s eyes,
and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went and washed, and came back seeing.
verse.note: Siloam was a pool at the southern end of Jerusalem, fed by a water channel from the Gihon spring. Its Hebrew name, Shiloah, resembles the Hebrew verb “to send,” and John’s gloss invites the reader to connect the pool with Jesus, who repeatedly describes himself in this Gospel as the one sent by the Father (as in verse 4).

verse.text: So the neighbors and those who used to see him before as a beggar said, “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?”
Some were saying, “This is the man.” Others were saying, “No, but he looks like him.” He himself kept saying, “I am the one.”
So they said to him, “How then were your eyes opened?”
He answered, “The man called Jesus made mud and smeared it on my eyes and said to me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed, and I gained my sight.”
They said to him, “Where is he?” He said, “I don’t know.”
They brought the man who had once been blind to the Pharisees.
Now it was a Sabbath on the day Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.
verse.note: The detail explains the Pharisees’ objection in verse 16. Kneading appears among the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath in later rabbinic lists, and healing a chronic, non-life-threatening condition on the Sabbath was widely considered impermissible. Making mud and healing a man blind from birth would have been seen as a breach on both counts.

verse.text: So the Pharisees also asked him again how he had gained his sight. He said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”
So some of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” Others said, “How can a man who is a sinner perform such signs?” And there was a division among them.
So they said to the blind man again, “What do you say about him, since it was your eyes he opened?” He said, “He is a prophet.”
The Jewish leaders did not believe that he had been blind and had gained his sight until they summoned the parents of the man who had gained his sight
verse.note: The Greek says simply “the Jews,” but everyone in this scene is Jewish, including the man, his parents and Jesus. The group meant is the authorities who conduct the inquiry (the Pharisees of verses 13–16) and who have power to expel people from the synagogue (verse 22). Scholars are divided over how best to render the term in John; this translation uses “the Jewish leaders” where the narrower group is clearly in view.

verse.text: and asked them, “Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”
His parents answered, “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind.

text.q: But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself.”

verse.text: His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders, for the Jewish leaders had already agreed that if anyone acknowledged him as the Messiah, that person would be put out of the synagogue.
verse.note: The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered “Christ.” Here it is not a name but a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and the question is whether Jesus is that figure. “Messiah” conveys this to a modern reader, and several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

The Greek is a single adjective found only in John’s Gospel (here and at 12:42 and 16:2). It means exclusion from the local Jewish community’s gathering, which carried heavy social as well as religious consequences. Scholars debate how formal such expulsion was in Jesus’s lifetime, and many think the wording also reflects the experience of John’s first readers later in the century.

verse.text: That is why his parents said, “He is of age; ask him.”
So for a second time they summoned the man who had been blind and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.”
verse.note: This is not an invitation to praise God for the healing but a solemn formula calling on someone to tell the truth or confess, as when Joshua says the same to Achan in Joshua 7:19. The authorities are putting the man on oath and pressing him to agree with their verdict on Jesus.

verse.text: He answered, “Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I know: I was blind, and now I see.”
So they said to him, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”
He answered them, “I told you already, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? You don’t want to become his disciples too, do you?”
They hurled abuse at him and said, “You are that man’s disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.

text.q: We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.”

verse.text: The man answered them, “Now here is the amazing thing: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes.

text.q: We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is devout and does his will, God listens to that person.
Since time began it has never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a person born blind.

verse.note: The Greek idiom is literally “from the age,” using a time-word, not the word for “world.” It means from the remote past or from the very beginning, and is rendered accordingly.

text.q: If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”

verse.text: They answered him, “You were born entirely in sins, and you are teaching us?” And they threw him out.
Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and when he found him he said, “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”
verse.note: The earliest and best manuscripts read “Son of Man”; many later manuscripts read “Son of God,” which is the reading of the King James Version. “Son of God” is generally regarded as a later change toward the more familiar confession, and modern editions read “Son of Man.”

verse.text: He answered, “And who is he, sir, so that I may believe in him?”
verse.note: The same Greek form of address appears in verse 36 and verse 38. It ranges from a polite “sir” to “Lord” as a confession. In verse 36 the man does not yet know who the Son of Man is, so “sir” fits; in verse 38 it accompanies belief and worship, so “Lord” is used. The Greek leaves the shift to the reader, and some translations use “Lord” in both verses.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.”
He said, “I believe, Lord,” and he worshiped him.
And Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind.”
Some of the Pharisees who were with him heard this and said to him, “Surely we are not blind too?”
Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin. But now you say, ‘We see.’ Your sin remains.”

text.q: “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate but climbs in some other way—that one is a thief and a bandit.

verse.note: Greek distinguishes the thief, who steals by stealth, from this word, which names an armed and violent plunderer such as a highwayman or brigand. “Robber” is the usual rendering and is not wrong, but in modern English it can suggest a burglar; “bandit” keeps the violence and outlawry. Standard lexicons give robber, highwayman or bandit, and note that the word was also applied to insurrectionists.

The Greek word covers any entrance that opens and shuts. The older English tradition has “door,” as in “I am the door” (verses 7 and 9); because the picture here is the entrance to a walled sheep enclosure, “gate” is the natural English word, and several modern translations use it. The meaning is not in dispute.

text.q: But the one who enters through the gate is the shepherd of the sheep.
The gatekeeper opens for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
When he has brought out all his own, he goes ahead of them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.
A stranger they will never follow; they will run away from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.”

verse.text: Jesus told them this figure of speech, but they did not understand what it was that he was saying to them.
verse.note: John does not use the word for “parable” found in the other Gospels. His word means a proverb or a veiled, figurative saying, and he later contrasts it with speaking “plainly” (16:25, 29). Older versions have “parable” here; most modern ones have “figure of speech.”

verse.text: So Jesus said to them again, “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep.

text.q: All who came before me are thieves and bandits, but the sheep did not listen to them.
I am the gate. Whoever enters through me will be saved, and will come in and go out and find pasture.
The thief comes only to steal and slaughter and destroy. I came so that they may have life, and have it in abundance.
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
The hired hand, who is not a shepherd and does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and runs away, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them.
He runs away because he is a hired hand and does not care about the sheep.
I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me,
just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep.
I have other sheep too, which are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice, and there will be one flock, one shepherd.
This is why the Father loves me: I lay down my life so that I may take it up again.
No one takes it from me; I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This command I received from my Father.”

verse.text: Again there was a division among the Jews because of these words.
verse.note: John often uses this term for a particular group in Jerusalem that disputes with Jesus, not for the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus, his disciples and those who defend him in verse 21 are also Jews. Here and in verses 24–33 the group is not clearly identified as the authorities, so the general term is kept. Some scholars prefer “Judeans” or “the Jewish leaders” in such passages.

verse.text: Many of them were saying, “He has a demon and is out of his mind! Why listen to him?”
Others were saying, “These are not the words of someone possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?”
Then came the Festival of Dedication in Jerusalem. It was winter,
verse.note: This is the festival now known as Hanukkah. It commemorates the rededication of the Jerusalem temple in 164 BC, after its desecration under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV. It lasts eight days and falls in December, hence “it was winter.”

verse.text: and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s Colonnade.
So the Jews surrounded him and said to him, “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.”

note.traditional: make us to doubt; keep us in suspense

verse.note: The Greek idiom is literally “How long are you lifting up our life?” Nearly all modern translations understand it as holding someone in suspense. Evidence for the idiom outside this verse is thin, and some interpreters take it instead as “How long will you annoy us?”

The Greek word translates the Hebrew title for the anointed king Israel expected. Here the questioners are asking about that title, not using a name, so “Messiah” conveys what they meant. Several modern translations use “Messiah” in such places in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it functions as a name.

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name—these testify about me;

text.q: but you do not believe, because you do not belong to my sheep.
My sheep listen to my voice; I know them, and they follow me.
I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.
As for what my Father has given me, he is greater than all, and no one can snatch it out of the Father’s hand.

note.term: As for what my Father has given me, he is greater than all
note.traditional: My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all

verse.note: The manuscripts differ here in two small words, giving either “My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all” (the reading most English versions follow) or “What my Father has given me is greater than all.” The Greek text followed here combines a neuter “what” with a masculine “greater,” which is grammatically rough. The rendering keeps both: “what my Father has given me” is set out in front as the topic, and “greater” is taken as describing the Father. The Greek gives no object for “snatch”; the “it” is supplied and refers back to what the Father has given.

text.q: I and the Father are one.”

verse.note: The Greek word for “one” is neuter: “one thing,” not “one person.” In context the claim concerns unity in keeping the sheep, since no one can snatch them from either hand, and the hearers take it as a claim to divine status (verse 33). How far the statement reaches beyond unity of action and purpose toward unity of being has been debated since antiquity.

verse.text: Again the Jews picked up stones to stone him.
Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these works are you stoning me?”
The Jews answered him, “We are not stoning you for a good work but for blasphemy, because you, a human being, make yourself God.”
verse.note: The Greek has no article, so the phrase can be read “make yourself God” or “make yourself a god.” Most translations choose “God,” which fits the charge of blasphemy. Jesus’s reply in verses 34–36 turns on the plural “gods,” which suggests the looser sense is also in view.

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, you are gods’?
verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 82:6, so “Law” here stands for the Scriptures as a whole, not only the books of Moses. In the psalm God addresses a group as “gods”; ancient and modern interpreters have identified them variously as Israel’s judges, members of a heavenly council, or Israel receiving the Law at Sinai. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if Scripture can use the word of them, it is not blasphemy for the one the Father sent to call himself God’s Son.

text.q: If he called them ‘gods’ to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken,
do you say to the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am God’s Son’?

verse.note: The verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy” and means to bring someone or something into the sphere of what belongs to God. Here the point is that the Father set Jesus apart for a mission, not that he changed his moral state, so “consecrated” is used in place of the traditional “sanctified.” Several modern translations render it “consecrated” or “set apart” in this verse; the meaning is not disputed.

text.q: If I am not doing the works of my Father, do not believe me.
But if I am doing them, then even if you do not believe me, believe the works, so that you may come to know and keep on knowing that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”

note.term: come to know and keep on knowing

verse.note: The Greek uses the same verb twice in two different forms, the first pointing to the moment of coming to know and the second to knowing as a continuing state. Most translations vary the English (“know and understand”); this rendering keeps the repetition. Some manuscripts replace the second verb with “believe.”

verse.text: So they were again trying to seize him, but he escaped from their hands.
He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing, and he stayed there.
Many came to him and were saying, “John performed no sign, but everything John said about this man was true.”
And many believed in him there.
Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.
This Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with perfume and wiped his feet with her hair; it was her brother Lazarus who was ill.

note.term: the one who anointed the Lord with perfume

verse.note: The anointing is not narrated until the next chapter (12:1–8). The narrator identifies Mary by it here, which suggests the story was already well known to the first readers.

verse.text: So the sisters sent word to him, saying, “Lord, look, the one you love is ill.”
When Jesus heard it, he said, “This illness is not to end in death, but is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”
Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.
So when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he then stayed two days in the place where he was.
Then, after this, he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”
The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, just now the Judeans were trying to stone you, and you are going back there?”
verse.note: The Greek word can mean both “Jews” and “Judeans.” Here the point is geographic: Jesus has just proposed returning to Judea, and the disciples, themselves Jews, object that people there had tried to stone him. Elsewhere in the chapter the word is rendered “Jews.” Scholars are divided on how far “Judeans” should be used in John.

verse.text: Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, they do not stumble, because they see the light of this world.

text.q: But if anyone walks in the night, they stumble, because the light is not in them.”

verse.text: He said these things, and after this he told them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to wake him.”
So the disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for “save,” used for rescue and healing as well as for salvation. The disciples mean only that sleep is a good sign in a sick man. A reader of John may also hear the fuller sense “he will be saved.”

verse.text: Now Jesus had spoken about his death, but they thought he was speaking of resting in sleep.
So then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,

text.q: and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”

verse.text: So Thomas, who was called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us go too, so that we may die with him.”
When Jesus arrived, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.
Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles away,
verse.note: The Greek says “about fifteen stadia.” A stadion was roughly 185 meters (about 600 feet), so the distance is a little under two miles, or about three kilometers.

verse.text: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them about their brother.
So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went to meet him, but Mary stayed sitting in the house.
Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.

text.q: And even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”
Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if they die, will live,

text.q: and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?”

verse.text: She said to him, “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one who is coming into the world.”
verse.note: The Greek word means “anointed one” and translates the Hebrew title “Messiah,” the king Israel expected. Martha is confessing a title, not using a name, so “Messiah” is used here, as in several modern translations. “Christ” is kept where the word functions as a name.

verse.text: When she had said this, she went away and called her sister Mary, saying privately, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”
When Mary heard this, she got up quickly and went to him.
Now Jesus had not yet come into the village but was still at the place where Martha had met him.
The Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary get up quickly and go out, and they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.
When Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”
When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping, he was stirred with anger in his spirit and deeply troubled,

note.term: was stirred with anger in his spirit
note.traditional: was deeply moved in spirit (KJV: groaned in the spirit)

verse.note: Outside this chapter the verb is used of stern warning or indignant scolding (Mark 1:43; 14:5), and in wider Greek of angry snorting. It does not elsewhere mean grief or tenderness. Most English versions soften it to “deeply moved,” but many commentators hold that anger or indignation is meant, whether at death itself or at the unbelief around him; the text does not say which. The same verb recurs in verse 38.

verse.text: and he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”
Jesus wept.
verse.note: The verb is not the one used for Mary and the mourners in verses 31 and 33, which often implies loud lament. This one, found only here in the New Testament, means to shed tears. Many take its tense to mean “burst into tears.”

verse.text: So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”
But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man have done something so that this man too would not die?”
Then Jesus, again stirred with anger within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by now there is a stench, for it has been four days.”

note.traditional: he hath been dead four days

verse.note: Burial normally took place on the day of death. Later rabbinic tradition records a belief that the soul lingered near the body for three days. It is uncertain whether this belief was current in Jesus’s time, but the fourth day in any case puts the death beyond all doubt.

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believe you will see the glory of God?”
So they took away the stone. And Jesus raised his eyes upward and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.

text.q: I knew that you always hear me, but I said this for the sake of the crowd standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

verse.text: When he had said this, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!”
The dead man came out, his feet and hands bound with strips of cloth and his face wrapped in a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Untie him and let him go.”
So many of the Jews, those who had come to Mary and seen what he did, believed in him.
But some of them went off to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
So the chief priests and the Pharisees convened a meeting of the council and said, “What are we doing? For this man is performing many signs.

text.q: If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”

verse.note: “Place” most likely means the temple, which was commonly called “the place” or “the holy place.” It could also mean Jerusalem, or the council’s own position and standing. The literal word is kept so that the reader can weigh these.

The Greek word is the one translated “Gentiles” elsewhere when it is plural and refers to the non-Jewish peoples. In the singular it means a people as a national unit, here the Jewish nation. In verse 50 Caiaphas sets it beside a different word, “people,” the usual scriptural term for Israel as God’s people.

verse.text: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all,

note.traditional: the high priest that same year

verse.note: The high priesthood was not an annual office; Caiaphas held it for nearly two decades, from about AD 18 to 36. “That year” most likely means “in that fateful year,” the year of Jesus’s death. The same Greek word in the plural is rendered “chief priests,” meaning the leading priestly families.

text.q: nor do you consider that it is to your advantage that one man should die for the people and the whole nation not perish.”

verse.text: He did not say this on his own, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation,
and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God.
So from that day on they planned to kill him.
So Jesus no longer walked about openly among the Jews, but went away from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.
Now the Passover of the Jews was near, and many went up to Jerusalem from the countryside before the Passover to purify themselves.
So they were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the festival?”
Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that anyone who knew where he was should report it, so that they might arrest him.
Then, six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.
So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha was serving, and Lazarus was one of those reclining at table with him.
Then Mary took a pound of perfume—pure nard, very costly—and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. And the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.
verse.note: The measure is the Roman pound, about twelve ounces or a little under 330 grams. Nard was an imported aromatic oil. The price Judas names in verse 5, three hundred denarii, was roughly a year’s wages for a laborer, since a denarius was a common day’s pay.

The Greek adjective is rare and its exact meaning is uncertain. Most scholars take it as “genuine” or “unadulterated”, which is followed here. Other proposals are that it names the plant or place the nard came from, or that it means “liquid”. The same phrase occurs in Mark 14:3.

verse.text: But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples, the one who was going to hand him over, said,
verse.note: Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing someone into another’s custody, and the Gospels use it equally of the priests and of Pilate. “Hand over” lets the reader see that chain; the treachery is supplied by the context. Some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual sense for Judas.

text.q: “Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”

verse.text: He said this not because he cared about the poor but because he was a thief; he kept the money box and used to take what was put into it.

note.term: used to take what was put into it

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means “carry”, and the clause could say only that Judas carried the common funds. In the Greek of the period it was also used for carrying off or pilfering. After “he was a thief” that sense is likely, and most modern translations adopt it.

verse.text: So Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.

note.term: so that she may keep it for the day of my burial
note.traditional: against the day of my burying hath she kept this

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and its sense is disputed. It may mean “let her keep it” (what remains) for the burial. Or it may be elliptical: she did not sell it so that she could keep it for this purpose, with the anointing itself anticipating the burial. Some later manuscripts smooth the wording to “she has kept it”.

text.q: For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.”

verse.text: Then a large crowd of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came not only because of Jesus but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.
So the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well,
because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
The next day the large crowd that had come to the festival, hearing that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem,
took palm branches and went out to meet him, and they were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord, the king of Israel!”
verse.note: The word is a Hebrew cry meaning “save, please”, taken from Psalm 118:25. By the first century it was used as a shout of acclamation. The crowd’s words draw on Psalm 118:25–26, a psalm sung at the pilgrim festivals, and add “the king of Israel”. Palm branches were associated with national celebration and victory.

verse.text: Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written:

text.q: “Do not be afraid, daughter of Zion. Look, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt.”

verse.text: His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and that they had done these things for him.
So the crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead kept testifying.
This was also why the crowd went to meet him: they had heard that he had done this sign.
So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see that you are getting nowhere. Look, the world has gone after him!”
Now there were some Greeks among those who went up to worship at the festival.
These came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and made a request of him: “Sir, we want to see Jesus.”
Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus.
Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
Whoever loves their life loses it, and whoever hates their life in this world will keep it for eternal life.

verse.note: In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, different in kind as well as unending. The word for “life” in this phrase is not the same as the “life” that is loved or hated earlier in the verse. That earlier word means a person’s present life or living self, which can be clung to and lost.

text.q: If anyone serves me, they must follow me, and where I am, there my servant will be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor them.
Now my soul is troubled, and what should I say? ‘Father, save me from this hour’? But it was for this very reason that I came to this hour.

note.term: Father, save me from this hour
note.traditional: Father, save me from this hour

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation. The words may be a hypothetical prayer that Jesus considers and sets aside, as punctuated here, or an actual prayer that he then corrects with “But it was for this very reason…”. Translations and commentators are divided.

verse.text: Father, glorify your name.” Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”
The crowd standing there heard it and said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”
Jesus answered, “This voice came not for my sake but for yours.

text.q: Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be thrown out.
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”

verse.note: The verb means both to raise physically and to exalt. John uses it with both senses at once: Jesus is raised up on the cross, and the cross is his exaltation. Verse 33 makes the reference to crucifixion explicit. Some manuscripts read “all things” in place of “all people”.

verse.text: He said this to indicate what kind of death he was going to die.
So the crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Messiah remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?”
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “the Christ”. Here the crowd is debating what the expected anointed king will be like, so the word is a title, not a name, and “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

“The Law” here stands for the Scriptures as a whole, not only the books of Moses. No single passage says this in so many words. The crowd is probably thinking of promises that David’s line and kingdom will endure forever, such as Psalm 89:36.

verse.text: So Jesus said to them, “The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, so that darkness does not overtake you. Whoever walks in the darkness does not know where they are going.
While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become children of light.” Jesus said these things, then went away and hid himself from them.
Though he had done so many signs in front of them, they did not believe in him,
so that the word that Isaiah the prophet spoke would be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”
This is why they were unable to believe, because Isaiah also said:

text.q: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they would not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.”

verse.text: Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke about him.
verse.note: The quotation in verse 40 comes from Isaiah 6, where the prophet sees the Lord enthroned in the temple. John says that the glory Isaiah saw there was that of Jesus, who is the “him” of this verse. Some manuscripts read “when he saw” in place of “because he saw”.

verse.text: Nevertheless, many even among the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they would not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue,
for they loved the glory that comes from people more than the glory that comes from God.
Then Jesus cried out, “Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in the one who sent me,

text.q: and whoever sees me sees the one who sent me.
I have come into the world as light, so that everyone who believes in me would not remain in the darkness.
If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge that person, for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.
Whoever rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge: the word that I have spoken will judge that person on the last day.
For I have not spoken on my own; the Father who sent me has himself given me a command—what to say and what to speak.
And I know that his command is eternal life. So what I speak, I speak just as the Father has told me.”

verse.text: Now before the Passover festival, Jesus knew that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean “to the end” in time (to the last moment of his life) or “to the utmost,” that is, completely. Many interpreters think John intends both, and the phrase is echoed in Jesus’s final word from the cross, “It is finished” (19:30). “To the end” is kept because English can hear both senses in it.

verse.text: During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to hand him over,
verse.note: Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing someone into another’s custody, and the Gospels use the same verb for what the chief priests and Pilate later do to Jesus. “Hand over” lets that chain show. The treachery comes from the context, though some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual sense.

note.traditional: put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him

verse.note: The best-attested Greek text says literally that the devil had already put “into the heart that Judas son of Simon Iscariot should hand him over,” without saying whose heart. Most translations take it as Judas’s heart, as here. Some scholars read it as the devil’s own heart, meaning the devil had already resolved that Judas would do this, with Satan entering Judas only at verse 27. Later manuscripts adjust the grammar so that the heart is plainly Judas’s.

verse.text: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God,
got up from supper, laid down his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.
verse.note: The verbs for “laying down” the garments here and “taking them up” in verse 12 are the ones Jesus uses in 10:17–18 for laying down his life and taking it up again, and Peter uses the first in verse 37. Many commentators think the echo is deliberate, so the translation keeps the same English verbs, though not all agree that John intends a symbol here.

verse.text: Then he poured water into the basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to dry them with the towel he had tied around him.
So he came to Simon Peter, who said to him, “Lord, are you going to wash my feet?”
Jesus answered him, “What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will understand.”
Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!” Jesus answered him, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
Jesus said to him, “The one who has bathed has no need to wash anything except the feet, but is clean all over. And you are clean, but not all of you.”
verse.note: A few early witnesses lack the words “except the feet,” giving “The one who has bathed has no need to wash, but is clean all over.” Most manuscripts include the words, as does the Greek text translated here. Scholars are divided over which form is original.

verse.text: For he knew who was handing him over; that is why he said, “Not all of you are clean.”
So when he had washed their feet and taken up his outer garments and reclined at the table again, he said to them, “Do you understand what I have done for you?

text.q: You call me ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord,’ and you are right to say so, for I am.
So if I, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, so that you also should do just as I have done for you.
Truly, truly, I tell you, a slave is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired servant, and “master” here is the same Greek word translated “Lord” in verses 13–14. Many English versions soften it to “servant.” Several recent translations use “slave,” as here.

The Greek word is the one usually rendered “apostle,” and this is its only occurrence in John’s Gospel. Here it has its ordinary sense of someone sent on another’s behalf, paired with “the one who sent him.”

text.q: If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.
I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But this is so that the Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘The one who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me.’

note.term: has lifted his heel against me

verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 41:9, where the psalmist laments being turned on by a close friend who shared his table. In the ancient world eating someone’s bread created a bond of loyalty, so an attack from a table companion was an especially bitter treachery. The exact picture behind “lifting the heel” is uncertain; it may be a kick or a gesture of contempt.

text.q: I am telling you this now, before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe that I am he.

verse.note: The Greek is simply “I am,” with no “he.” It can be an everyday way of saying “I am the one,” but in the Greek version of Isaiah (for example 43:10, “that you may know and believe … that I am”) it is God’s own self-declaration. Many scholars think John intends that echo here. Others take it more simply as “that I am who I claim to be.”

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever receives anyone I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”

verse.text: After saying this, Jesus was troubled in spirit and testified, “Truly, truly, I tell you, one of you will hand me over.”
The disciples looked at one another, at a loss as to which one he meant.
One of his disciples, the one Jesus loved, was reclining at the table at Jesus’s side.
verse.note: Guests at a formal meal reclined on their left side on cushions, so that the head of one diner lay near the chest of the person to his left. The Greek says this disciple was reclining “in the bosom of Jesus,” the place of a close companion, and John uses the same word in 1:18 for the Son’s closeness to the Father. “Bosom” is no longer natural English.

verse.text: So Simon Peter nodded to this disciple to ask who it was that he was speaking about.
Leaning back, just as he was, against Jesus’s chest, that disciple said to him, “Lord, who is it?”
Jesus answered, “It is the one for whom I will dip the piece of bread and give it to him.” So he dipped the piece of bread and gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot.
And after the piece of bread, Satan then entered into him. So Jesus said to him, “What you are doing, do quickly.”
But none of those reclining at the table knew why he said this to him.
Some thought that, since Judas kept the money box, Jesus was telling him to buy what they needed for the festival, or to give something to the poor.
So after taking the piece of bread, he went out at once. And it was night.
When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.

text.q: If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him at once.

note.term: If God has been glorified in him,

verse.note: This opening clause is missing from several of the earliest and most important manuscripts and present in the majority of later ones. It may have been dropped accidentally because it repeats the end of the previous sentence, or added to smooth the logic. The Greek text translated here includes it, and the sense of the passage is little affected either way.

text.q: Little children, I am with you only a little while longer. You will look for me, and just as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so now I say it to you too.
I give you a new commandment: that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

verse.text: Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow later.”
Peter said to him, “Lord, why can’t I follow you right now? I will lay down my life for you.”
Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I tell you, a rooster will not crow until you have denied me three times.”

text.q: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me.

note.term: Believe in God; believe also in me.
note.traditional: ye believe in God, believe also in me

verse.note: The Greek verb form is the same for a statement (“you believe”) and a command (“believe”), and it occurs twice. The line can therefore be read as two commands, as here, or as “You believe in God; believe also in me,” or even as two statements. Most recent translations and commentators take both as commands, which suits the opening “Do not let your hearts be troubled.”

text.q: In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places. If there were not, I would have told you, because I am going to prepare a place for you.

verse.note: The Greek noun means a place where one stays or lives and is related to the verb translated “remain” throughout this chapter. “Mansions” comes from the Latin translation, where the word meant a lodging, and now wrongly suggests a grand house. Many modern versions have “rooms.” “Dwelling places” is used here so that the link with verse 23, where the same noun is rendered “dwelling,” stays visible.

note.term: I would have told you, because I am going
note.traditional: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you

verse.note: The Greek can be punctuated in more than one way. It may be a question: “If there were not, would I have told you that I am going to prepare a place for you?” Many recent versions take it so. This translation follows the punctuation of the edition being translated, which reads it as a statement, and takes the connecting word as “because.”

text.q: And if I go and prepare a place for you, I am coming again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.
And you know the way to where I am going.”

verse.text: Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”
Jesus said to him, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.

text.q: If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you know him and have seen him.”

note.term: If you had known me, you would have known my Father also.
note.traditional: If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also

verse.note: Manuscripts differ here. The reading translated is a mild rebuke that implies the disciples have not really known Jesus. Other early manuscripts read “If you have come to know me, you will know my Father also,” which is a promise. Scholars are divided over which is original.

verse.text: Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.”
Jesus said to him, “Have I been with all of you for so long, and you have not come to know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?

text.q: Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own; the Father who remains in me does his works.
Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me; or else, believe because of the works themselves.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.
And whatever you ask in my name, that I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it.

note.traditional: If ye shall ask any thing in my name

verse.note: Some manuscripts lack “me,” and a few omit the whole verse, probably because it seemed to repeat verse 13. The reading with “me,” in which prayer is addressed to Jesus himself, has strong early support and is the one translated.

text.q: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments.
And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, to be with you forever—

verse.note: Outside the New Testament the word is used of someone called in to speak or act on another’s behalf, and 1 John 2:1 uses it of Jesus in just that sense. “Comforter” goes back to early English versions and is narrower than the Greek. “Advocate,” “Helper” and “Counselor” are all in current use among translators. “Another” implies that Jesus himself has been filling this role for the disciples.

text.q: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, because he remains with you and will be in you.

verse.note: The Greek word for “Spirit” is grammatically neuter, and the pronouns in this verse are neuter to agree with it. In verse 26 the pronoun is masculine, agreeing with the masculine noun for “Advocate.” Greek grammatical gender does not itself indicate personhood. English “whom” and “him” follow the long-standing tradition and fit the personal role the Spirit is given in this passage.

text.q: I will not leave you orphans; I am coming to you.
In a little while the world will no longer see me, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live.

note.term: but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live.
note.traditional: but ye see me: because I live, ye shall live also

verse.note: The Greek can also be read as one sentence: “but you will see me, because I live and you will live.” On that reading the disciples’ seeing Jesus is grounded in his life and theirs. The translation follows the more common division, which makes “Because I live, you also will live” a separate promise.

text.q: On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.
Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. And the one who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I too will love them and reveal myself to them.”

verse.text: Judas—not Iscariot—said to him, “Lord, what has happened, that you are going to reveal yourself to us and not to the world?”
Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, they will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our dwelling with them.

text.q: Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but belongs to the Father who sent me.
“I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you.
But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name—he will teach you everything and remind you of everything I have said to you.
Peace I leave with you; my own peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not let them lose courage.

verse.note: This verb is not the ordinary Greek word for fear. It means to be timid or cowardly, to lose one’s nerve. The Greek Old Testament uses it in exhortations such as those to Joshua not to be dismayed before a daunting task. Most English versions have simply “be afraid.”

text.q: You heard me tell you, ‘I am going away, and I am coming to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I am.
And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe.
I will not speak with you much longer, for the ruler of the world is coming. He has no claim on me,

note.term: He has no claim on me

verse.note: The Greek is literally “in me he has nothing.” Most interpreters take this as an idiom meaning that the ruler of the world has no claim on Jesus or hold over him, perhaps reflecting a Semitic legal expression. Several modern versions also render it “no claim on me” or “no power over me.”

text.q: but so that the world may know that I love the Father, I do just as the Father commanded me. Get up; let us go from here.”

note.term: but so that the world may know
note.traditional: But that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do

verse.note: The Greek sentence is compressed and has no stated main clause before “so that.” It can be read as here, with “I do just as the Father commanded me” as the main statement. It can also be read as “but this happens so that the world may know that I love the Father and that I do just as the Father commanded me.” The sense differs only slightly.

note.term: Get up; let us go from here.

verse.note: Jesus’ speech nevertheless continues for three more chapters, and the group is not said to leave until 18:1. Some scholars think the following chapters were spoken on the way. Others think the line marks a seam where different blocks of discourse were joined, or that it is a summons to face what is coming rather than to leave the room. The question is unresolved.

text.q: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinegrower.

verse.note: In Israel’s Scriptures the vine or vineyard is a standing image for Israel itself, planted and tended by God and often faulted for failing to yield good fruit (for example Psalm 80 and Isaiah 5). A first-century Jewish reader would hear “the true vine” against that background. The speech continues from chapter 14 and runs on into chapter 16, so the quotation marks do not close at the end of this chapter.

text.q: Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes clean so that it may bear more fruit.

verse.note: The verb can mean either “remove” or “lift up,” and a minority of interpreters think the vinegrower is lifting trailing branches off the ground so that they can bear. Most scholars take it as removal, which fits the discarded and burned branches of verse 6. That is the reading followed here.

The Greek verb means “to clean” and was used for clearing or pruning plants. It echoes “takes away” in sound (airei, kathairei), and it leads straight into “you are already clean” (katharoi) in verse 3. Most versions have simply “prunes,” which hides the link; “prunes clean” keeps the connection visible.

text.q: You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you.
Remain in me, and I in you. Just as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me.

verse.note: The traditional “abide” is now rare outside religious language. The Greek is the ordinary verb for staying or remaining somewhere, and “remain” is used for it throughout this chapter, including for the fruit in verse 16. Several modern versions do the same; others keep “abide.”

text.q: I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, is the one who bears much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
If anyone does not remain in me, that person is thrown out like a branch and withers; such branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.
If you remain in me and my words remain in you, ask for whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.
In this my Father is glorified: that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.

note.traditional: so prove to be my disciples

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means “become,” but it can also mean “turn out to be,” and many versions render “prove to be my disciples,” since the hearers already are disciples. Manuscripts are also divided between “and become” and “and you will become.” The plainer “become” is kept here; on this reading discipleship is something one keeps growing into.

text.q: As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you. Remain in my love.
If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.
I have spoken these things to you so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be made full.
“This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you.
No one has greater love than this: to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
You are my friends if you do what I command you.
I no longer call you slaves, because the slave does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I heard from my Father I have made known to you.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. The contrast depends on this: a slave is given orders without explanations, while a friend is taken into confidence. Many traditional versions have “servants”; a number of recent ones use “slaves.”

text.q: You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and for your fruit to remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name he may give you.
These things I command you so that you will love one another.

note.term: so that you will love one another
note.traditional: These things I command you, that ye love one another

verse.note: The Greek can be read as giving the purpose of the commands (“I command you these things so that you will love one another”) or their content (“This is what I command you: love one another”). The plural “these things” slightly favors the first reading, which is followed here. Verse 12 clearly uses the same construction for content, and several versions take this verse that way as well.

text.q: “If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before you.

verse.note: The Greek form can be a command (“know”) or a statement (“you know”). Most modern versions take it as a command, as here.

text.q: If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world—that is why the world hates you.
Remember the word that I spoke to you: ‘A slave is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will also keep yours.
But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know the one who sent me.
If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.
Whoever hates me hates my Father too.
If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would have no sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father.
But this happened so that the word written in their Law might be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without cause.’

verse.note: The words quoted come from the Psalms (see Psalms 35:19 and 69:4), not from the books of Moses. “Law” is used here in the broad sense, current at the time, of the Scriptures as a whole. “Their Law” points out that the Scripture the opponents themselves claim testifies against them.

text.q: “When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who comes out from the Father—he will testify about me.

verse.note: The traditional “Comforter” goes back to early English versions. Outside the New Testament the word is used of someone who speaks on another’s behalf, and 1 John 2:1 clearly uses it that way. That sense fits the testifying role described here. “Advocate,” “Helper,” and “Counselor” are all in current use among translations.

text.q: And you also testify, because you have been with me from the beginning.

verse.note: The Greek form can be a statement (“you are testifying”) or a command (“you too must testify”), and versions differ; some render it as a future. The English here is left open in the same way as the Greek.

text.q: “I have said these things to you so that you will not fall away.

verse.note: The verb pictures someone being tripped up so that they fall from loyalty to God. The older rendering “be offended” now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak; here Jesus is warning against abandoning him under persecution. Most modern versions also have “fall away” or “stumble” in this verse.

text.q: They will put you out of the synagogue; indeed, an hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think they are offering worship to God.

note.term: put you out of the synagogue

verse.note: The Greek is a single adjective meaning “expelled from the synagogue,” found in the New Testament only in John. For a first-century Jew this meant exclusion from the community's worship and much of its social life, not merely from a building. What formal procedure, if any, lies behind the term is debated.

text.q: And they will do these things because they have not known the Father or me.
But I have said these things to you so that when their hour comes you will remember that I told you about them. I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.
“But now I am going to the one who sent me, and none of you asks me, ‘Where are you going?’
Instead, because I have said these things to you, pain has filled your hearts.

verse.note: The Greek word covers both grief and physical pain, and Jesus uses it of the disciples' grief (verses 6, 20, 22) and of a woman's labor (verse 21). “Pain” is used throughout so that the comparison rests on one word in English as it does in Greek. Most versions have “sorrow” or “grief” for the disciples, and some switch to “pain” for the woman.

text.q: But I am telling you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.

verse.note: In the Greek of the period the word describes someone called in to help, especially one who speaks on another's behalf, and 1 John 2:1 uses it in that way of Jesus. “Comforter” comes from older English versions; “Advocate,” “Helper” and “Counselor” are all in current use. The courtroom tone suits what follows, where the Advocate proves the world wrong.

text.q: And when he comes, he will prove the world wrong about sin and about righteousness and about judgment:

verse.note: The verb means to expose, to show someone to be in the wrong, or to convict. Many versions have “convict the world concerning sin,” which could suggest bringing the world to feel its guilt; the rendering here takes it as demonstrating that the world's verdicts on sin, righteousness and judgment are mistaken. Both readings are widely held, and whether the world itself is persuaded is left open by the Greek.

text.q: about sin, because they do not believe in me;
about righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you will no longer see me;

verse.note: Whose righteousness is meant is not stated. The most common view is that it is Jesus' own: his return to the Father shows that he, condemned by the world as a wrongdoer, was in the right. Others take it as the righteousness the world falsely claims for itself, or the righteousness now made available to believers.

text.q: and about judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged.
“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.
But when he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you in all the truth; for he will not speak on his own, but will speak whatever he hears, and he will declare to you the things that are coming.

verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between “in all the truth” and “into all the truth.” The Greek text translated here reads “in”; the familiar “into all truth” follows the other reading. The difference in meaning is slight: guidance within the whole sphere of truth versus guidance toward it.

text.q: He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and declare it to you.
Everything the Father has is mine; that is why I said that he takes from what is mine and will declare it to you.
“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.”

verse.text: So some of his disciples said to one another, “What is this that he is telling us: ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’? And, ‘Because I am going to the Father’?”
So they kept saying, “What is this ‘little while’ he speaks of? We do not know what he is talking about.”

Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, and he said to them, “Are you questioning one another about this—that I said, ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’?

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.

When a woman is in labor she has pain, because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world.
So you too have pain now; but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy away from you.
And on that day you will ask me nothing. Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father for, he will give you in my name.

verse.note: This verse uses two different Greek verbs that both come out as “ask” in English. The first usually means to ask a question in John, though it can also mean to make a request (as in verse 26); the second means to ask for something. The likely sense is that on that day the disciples will have no more puzzled questions for Jesus, as in verses 17–19, but some take it as “you will request nothing from me.”

note.term: he will give you in my name
note.traditional: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you

verse.note: Manuscripts differ in word order. In the Greek text translated here, “in my name” follows “he will give you” and so describes the giving; in many other manuscripts it follows “ask the Father” and describes the asking, as in verse 24. Most English versions follow the second order.

text.q: Until now you have asked for nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.
“I have said these things to you in figures of speech. An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father.
On that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;
for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.
I came from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and going to the Father.”

verse.text: His disciples said, “See, now you are speaking plainly and using no figure of speech.

text.q: Now we know that you know everything and have no need for anyone to ask you. By this we believe that you came from God.”

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?
verse.note: Ancient Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, and the words can be read as a question or as a statement: “Now you believe.” Either way, the next verse shows that Jesus regards their belief as about to be tested and found wanting.

text.q: Look, an hour is coming—indeed it has come—when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me.
I have said these things to you so that in me you may have peace. In the world you have affliction; but take courage: I have conquered the world.”

verse.note: The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression that bears down on people. “Tribulation” is now heard by many readers as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the Greek does. The same word is rendered “anguish” in verse 21, where it describes the pain of childbirth, not hardship imposed from outside.

The verb is the normal Greek word for winning a battle, a contest or a lawsuit, and is related to the word for “victory.” “Overcome” in modern English can suggest merely getting past a difficulty. The meaning is not disputed; several modern versions also use “conquered” here, and it shows the link with the victory language of 1 John and Revelation.

verse.text: Jesus said these things; then, lifting his eyes to heaven, he said, “Father, the hour has come. Glorify your Son, so that the Son may glorify you,

text.q: just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he may give eternal life to all those you have given him.

verse.note: “All flesh” is a Semitic idiom, familiar from the Greek Old Testament, for all humanity seen as mortal creatures. Some translations paraphrase it as “all people”; the idiom is kept here because the Greek has it.

The adjective comes from the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length. That fits verse 3, which defines it as knowing God, not as endless duration. “Eternal” is the standard rendering; a minority of translators render “life of the age to come.”

text.q: And this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and the one you sent, Jesus Christ.
I glorified you on earth by finishing the work you gave me to do.
And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory I had with you before the world existed.
I revealed your name to the people you gave me out of the world. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.

verse.note: In biblical usage a person’s name stands for the person as made known: their identity, character and authority. To reveal God’s name is to make God himself known, and to be kept “in your name” (verses 11–12) is to be kept within what that name stands for.

text.q: Now they know that everything you have given me is from you,
for the words you gave me I have given to them, and they received them and truly came to know that I came from you, and they believed that you sent me.
I am asking on their behalf. I am not asking on behalf of the world but on behalf of those you have given me, because they are yours,
and all that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them.
I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, so that they may be one just as we are.

note.traditional: those whom thou hast given me

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “your name, which you have given me,” here and in verse 12. Many later manuscripts read “those whom you have given me,” making the gift the disciples and not the name; this is the reading behind the King James Version. Most modern editions and translations follow the earlier reading.

text.q: While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I guarded them, and not one of them was lost except the son of destruction, so that the Scripture would be fulfilled.

verse.note: “Son of” is a Semitic idiom for someone who belongs to or is destined for a thing; the reference is to Judas. The Greek noun for “destruction” is from the same root as the verb “was lost” just before it, so the phrase echoes it: none was lost but the one who belonged to loss. The Scripture in view is not named; many think of the psalm about the betrayer quoted earlier at John 13:18.

text.q: But now I am coming to you, and I say these things in the world so that they may have my joy made full in themselves.
I have given them your word, and the world has hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.
I am not asking that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.

verse.note: The Greek form can be masculine (“the evil one,” meaning the devil) or neuter (“evil” in general). Most modern translations and commentators choose “the evil one,” in line with the same usage in 1 John, but “keep them from evil” is grammatically possible.

text.q: They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.
Consecrate them in the truth; your word is truth.

verse.note: The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy” (compare “Holy Father” in verse 11) and means to set someone apart as belonging to God. “Sanctify,” the traditional word, now suggests to many readers a process of moral improvement; here the point is dedication to a mission (verse 18) and, in verse 19, Jesus dedicating himself, probably as an offering. “Consecrate” is used in both verses to keep that link, as several modern translations do. The phrase “in the truth” can also be read “by the truth.”

text.q: Just as you sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world.
And for their sake I consecrate myself, so that they too may be consecrated in truth.

verse.note: Unlike verse 17, the Greek here has no article, so the phrase may mean “in the truth” (the same truth as in verse 17) or simply “truly, really consecrated.” The rendering leaves both possibilities open; most interpreters think the link with verse 17 is intended.

text.q: I am not asking on behalf of these only, but also on behalf of those who believe in me through their word,
that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me.

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “that they also may be one in us,” and this is the familiar wording of older translations. Several of the earliest witnesses lack “one” here, and the edition translated follows them; the word may have been added by copyists from the first clause of the verse.

text.q: The glory that you have given me I have given to them, so that they may be one just as we are one,
I in them and you in me, so that they may be made completely one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them just as you loved me.
Father, those you have given me—I want them also to be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory, which you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.
Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you, and these have come to know that you sent me.
I made your name known to them, and I will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

verse.text: After saying these things, Jesus went out with his disciples across the Kidron Valley, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered.
Now Judas, who was handing him over, also knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with his disciples.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody, and John uses the same word in this chapter for what the leaders do to Jesus before Pilate (verses 30, 35, 36). Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject, which names the treachery the context supplies but hides the chain of handings-over. Some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual sense; the standard lexicons give “hand over” as the basic meaning.

verse.text: So Judas took the cohort, along with officers from the chief priests and from the Pharisees, and came there with lanterns and torches and weapons.

note.traditional: a band of men; a detachment of soldiers

verse.note: The word is the regular Greek term for a Roman cohort, on paper about six hundred men, though it could be used of a smaller unit, and its commander in verse 12 bears the title of a Roman tribune. John thus pictures Roman troops from the Jerusalem garrison alongside the temple officers. How many soldiers were actually present is not stated.

verse.text: Then Jesus, knowing everything that was coming upon him, went out and said to them, “Who are you looking for?”
They answered him, “Jesus the Nazarene.” He said to them, “I am he.” And Judas, who was handing him over, was standing with them.
verse.note: The Greek is simply “I am,” which is the normal way to say “That’s me” but is also the phrase John’s Jesus uses in an absolute sense that echoes God’s self-declaration in the Greek Scriptures (as at John 8:58). The arresting party’s falling to the ground in verse 6 suggests John intends the second meaning to be heard behind the first. English cannot carry both at once; the ordinary sense is given in the text.

verse.text: So when he said to them, “I am he,” they drew back and fell to the ground.
So he asked them again, “Who are you looking for?” And they said, “Jesus the Nazarene.”
Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. So if you are looking for me, let these men go.”
This was to fulfill the word he had spoken: “Of those you have given me, I have not lost a single one.”
Then Simon Peter, who had a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s slave and cut off his right ear. The slave’s name was Malchus.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by another, not a hired employee, and first-century readers would have understood Malchus as part of the high priest’s household property. Older English versions soften this to “servant”; several modern versions use “slave” here.

verse.text: So Jesus said to Peter, “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup the Father has given me—am I not to drink it?”
So the cohort and its commander and the officers of the Jewish leaders arrested Jesus and bound him
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for “Jews,” and it is rendered that way in verses 20, 33, 35 and 39. In verses 12, 14, 31, 36 and 38, however, John uses it for the Jerusalem authorities who arrest and accuse Jesus, not for the Jewish people as a whole—Jesus, his disciples and the crowds are all Jews. Scholars are divided on how best to render John’s usage; some prefer “Judeans” throughout, others keep “Jews” everywhere.

verse.text: and led him first to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.
Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jewish leaders that it was better for one man to die for the people.
Simon Peter was following Jesus, and so was another disciple. That disciple was known to the high priest, and he went with Jesus into the high priest’s courtyard,
but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, the one known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the woman who kept the door, and brought Peter in.
Then the slave girl who kept the door said to Peter, “You aren’t also one of this man’s disciples, are you?” He said, “I am not.”
Now the slaves and the officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing there warming themselves. Peter too was with them, standing and warming himself.
Then the high priest questioned Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching.
verse.note: The questioner here is Annas, since Jesus is sent on to Caiaphas only in verse 24. Annas had held the office earlier and had been deposed by the Romans, but he remained the head of the leading priestly family and evidently kept the title in common usage. Caiaphas, his son-in-law, was the officiating high priest.

verse.text: Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I always taught in synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together, and I said nothing in secret.

text.q: Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I said to them. Look, they know what I said.”

verse.text: When he said this, one of the officers standing by gave Jesus a slap, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”
Jesus answered him, “If I spoke wrongly, testify about the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?”
Then Annas sent him, still bound, to Caiaphas the high priest.
Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You aren’t also one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”
One of the high priest’s slaves, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said, “Didn’t I see you in the garden with him?”
So Peter denied it again, and at once a rooster crowed.
Then they led Jesus from Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the headquarters, so that they would not be defiled but could eat the Passover.
verse.note: The Greek borrows the Latin word praetorium, the official residence of a Roman governor, here Pilate’s base while in Jerusalem. Many versions keep the Latin term; it is translated here because the word means nothing to most modern readers. Its exact location in Jerusalem is disputed.

Entering a Gentile’s residence was held to make a person ritually unclean and so unable to share in the festival meal. In John’s account the Passover meal still lies ahead on the morning of the trial, whereas the other three Gospels present the Last Supper as a Passover meal. How the two chronologies relate is a long-standing and unresolved question.

verse.text: So Pilate went out to them and said, “What charge do you bring against this man?”
They answered him, “If this man were not doing wrong, we would not have handed him over to you.”
So Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.” The Jewish leaders said to him, “We are not permitted to put anyone to death.”

note.term: We are not permitted to put anyone to death
