note.traditional: It is not lawful for us to put any man to death

verse.note: Under Roman rule in Judea the power to execute appears to have been reserved to the governor, though the extent of this restriction is debated by historians. John sees a deeper point in verse 32: a Roman execution meant crucifixion, which matches Jesus’s earlier saying about being “lifted up” (John 12:32–33).

verse.text: This was to fulfill the word Jesus had spoken, indicating what kind of death he was going to die.
So Pilate went back into the headquarters, summoned Jesus, and said to him, “Are you the king of the Jews?”
Jesus answered, “Are you saying this on your own, or did others tell you about me?”
Pilate answered, “I am not a Jew, am I? Your own nation and the chief priests handed you over to me. What have you done?”
verse.note: The same Greek word in the plural is usually translated “Gentiles,” meaning the non-Jewish peoples. Here, in the singular, it refers to the Jewish people as a nation, and Pilate uses it to distance himself from what he treats as an internal affair.

verse.text: Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not from this world. If my kingdom were from this world, my officers would be fighting so that I would not be handed over to the Jewish leaders. But as it is, my kingdom is not from here.”
verse.note: The Greek preposition expresses source or origin, and the closing clause of the verse restates the point as “not from here.” The traditional “of this world” can suggest that the kingdom has nothing to do with the world; the Greek says that its origin and authority do not come from the world. Several modern versions also read “from.”

Jesus uses the same word that John has used throughout the chapter for the officers of the chief priests who arrested him (verses 3, 12, 18, 22). Most versions switch to “servants” or “followers” here, which hides the echo: the leaders have their officers, and if Jesus’s kingship were of the same kind, his would be fighting too.

verse.text: So Pilate said to him, “So then, you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I have come into the world: to testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”

note.term: You say that I am a king
note.traditional: Thou sayest that I am a king

verse.note: The reply can be taken as a noncommittal “That is your word for it,” as an affirmation (“You are right to say that I am a king”), or, with different punctuation, as “You say so; because I am a king, for this I was born.” The text keeps the literal wording, which neither denies the title nor accepts it on Pilate’s terms. Most commentators see a qualified affirmation.

verse.text: Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” Having said this, he went out again to the Jewish leaders and said to them, “I find no basis for a charge against him.

text.q: But you have a custom that I release one person to you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the king of the Jews?”

verse.text: Then they shouted back, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a bandit.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes an armed, violent outlaw such as a brigand or highwayman, not a thief who steals by stealth. It was also applied to insurgents, and Mark and Luke connect Barabbas with an uprising, so some versions render it “rebel” or “revolutionary” here; that reading is possible but not certain. “Bandit” keeps the violence and outlawry without deciding the question.

verse.text: Then Pilate took Jesus and had him flogged.
The soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head, and they put a purple cloak around him,
and they came up to him again and again, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” and they slapped him in the face.
Pilate went outside again and said to them, “Look, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no basis for a charge against him.”
So Jesus came outside, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple cloak. And Pilate said to them, “Here is the man!”
When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they shouted, “Crucify! Crucify!” Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no basis for a charge against him.”
The Jewish leaders answered him, “We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die, because he made himself out to be the Son of God.”
verse.note: The Greek is “the Jews,” the traditional rendering. In John’s trial narrative the group pressing Pilate is the Jerusalem authorities—the chief priests and their officers named in verse 6—not the Jewish people as a whole, so the narrower phrase is used here and in verses 12, 14, 31, and 38. Scholars are divided over the word generally: some prefer “Judeans” throughout, while others object that this removes Jews from the New Testament.

verse.text: When Pilate heard this statement, he grew more afraid,
and he went back into the governor’s headquarters and said to Jesus, “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.
So Pilate said to him, “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?”
Jesus answered him, “You would have no authority over me at all if it had not been given to you from above. For this reason the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”
From then on Pilate tried to release him, but the Jewish leaders shouted, “If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Everyone who makes himself out to be a king opposes Caesar.”
verse.note: “Friend of Caesar” may be more than a figure of speech: the phrase was used of those who enjoyed the emperor’s recognized favor, and losing that standing could end a career. Whether Pilate formally held such a status is uncertain, but the threat of being reported to the emperor as disloyal is clear.

verse.text: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus outside and sat down on the judge’s seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, or in Hebrew, Gabbatha.

note.term: sat down on the judge’s seat
note.traditional: sat down on the judgment seat

verse.note: The Greek verb can also take an object, giving “seated him on the judge’s seat,” so that Pilate places Jesus there in mockery before saying “Here is your king.” Most translators and commentators take it as Pilate himself sitting to pronounce sentence, as here; a minority defend the other reading.

The Greek word means “in the language of the Hebrews” and in this period could cover Aramaic as well as Hebrew. Gabbatha and Golgotha (verse 17) are Aramaic in form, and some versions therefore translate “in Aramaic.”

verse.text: Now it was the day of Preparation for the Passover, and it was about noon. He said to the Jewish leaders, “Here is your king!”

note.term: the day of Preparation for the Passover

verse.note: “Preparation” was the ordinary name for Friday, the day before the Sabbath (see verse 31). The phrase can mean the day on which the Passover was prepared, that is, the day before the feast, or “the Friday of Passover week.” The first fits John 18:28, where the leaders have not yet eaten the Passover; the second is preferred by those who align John’s chronology with the other Gospels.

The Greek says “about the sixth hour.” Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is midday, whereas the literal phrase suggests six o’clock to a modern reader. A minority of scholars argue that John counts from midnight, partly to ease the difference from Mark 15:25, which puts the crucifixion at the third hour.

verse.text: So they shouted, “Take him away! Take him away! Crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your king?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar.”
Then he handed him over to them to be crucified. So they took charge of Jesus.
Carrying the cross himself, he went out to what is called the Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha,
where they crucified him, and with him two others, one on each side, with Jesus in the middle.
Pilate also had a notice written and put on the cross. It read, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”
Many of the Jews read this notice, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek.
So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, “Do not write ‘The King of the Jews,’ but that this man said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’”
Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”

When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his clothes and divided them into four shares, a share for each soldier; they also took his tunic. Now the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top down.

So they said to one another, “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it will be.” This was so that the Scripture would be fulfilled that says, “They divided my clothes among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.” So that is what the soldiers did.
But standing beside the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

note.term: his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene

verse.note: The Greek list can be read as naming four women or three, if “Mary of Clopas” identifies the sister just mentioned. Most scholars count four, since two sisters both named Mary would be unlikely. The Greek says only “Mary of Clopas”; “wife” is the usual inference, though “daughter” is possible.

verse.text: When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, “Woman, here is your son.”
verse.note: In Greek this was a normal and courteous way to address a woman, without the curtness the bare word has in English; Jesus addresses his mother the same way at John 2:4. It is nonetheless unusual from a son to his mother, and interpreters differ over what, if anything, it signals.

verse.text: Then he said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.
After this, knowing that everything was now finished, Jesus said, so that the Scripture would be completed, “I am thirsty.”
verse.note: Most versions have “fulfilled,” but the verb is not John’s usual word for fulfilling Scripture (used in verses 24 and 36); it is related to “finished” in this verse and verse 30 and means to bring to completion. The clause may attach to what follows, as here, with Jesus speaking so that Scripture is completed (Psalm 69:21 is usually suggested), or to what precedes: everything was finished so that Scripture would be completed.

verse.text: A jar full of sour wine was standing there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop stalk and held it to his mouth.
When Jesus had taken the sour wine, he said, “It is finished.” And bowing his head, he handed over his spirit.
verse.note: Most versions have “gave up his spirit.” The verb is the same one used throughout the passion narrative for handing Jesus over (verses 11 and 16), and it was not a stock Greek expression for dying; the rendering keeps that link and the sense of a deliberate act. To whom the spirit is handed is not stated; most interpreters understand the Father.

verse.text: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross during the Sabbath—for that Sabbath was a great day—the Jewish leaders asked Pilate to have their legs broken and the bodies taken away.
verse.note: Breaking the legs hastened death; the usual explanation is that the crucified could no longer push themselves up to breathe. The Law required that an executed body not be left hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and this Sabbath was especially solemn because it fell at Passover.

verse.text: So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man and of the other who had been crucified with him.
But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.
Instead, one of the soldiers stabbed his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.
The one who saw it has testified, and his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe.
verse.note: The Greek has an emphatic “that one knows.” It most naturally refers to the eyewitness himself, as rendered here. Some interpreters take “that one” as someone other than the witness—Christ or God—called on to confirm his testimony.

verse.text: For these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: “Not a bone of his will be broken.”

note.term: Not a bone of his will be broken

verse.note: The wording is closest to the rules for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12), though Psalm 34:20, about God guarding the righteous sufferer, is also possible. Many scholars think John intends both; the Passover reference fits the setting of this chapter.

verse.text: And again, another Scripture says, “They will look on the one they pierced.”

After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, though a secret one for fear of the Jewish leaders, asked Pilate to let him take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave permission. So he came and took away his body.
Nicodemus also came, the one who had first come to Jesus by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.
verse.note: The unit is the Roman pound, roughly a third of a kilogram, so the amount is about thirty-three kilograms, or some seventy-two modern pounds. It is an extravagant quantity, far beyond what an ordinary burial required.

verse.text: So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid.
So because it was the Jews’ day of Preparation, and since the tomb was nearby, they laid Jesus there.
On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.
So she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple, the one Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have put him.”
So Peter and the other disciple set out and were going to the tomb.
The two were running together, but the other disciple ran ahead, faster than Peter, and reached the tomb first.
Bending down to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in.
Then Simon Peter also came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there,
and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths but rolled up in a place by itself.
Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;
for they did not yet understand the Scripture that he must rise from the dead.
Then the disciples went back home.
But Mary stood outside by the tomb, weeping. As she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb,
and she saw two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had been lying, one at the head and one at the feet.
They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have put him.”
verse.note: In Greek this was an ordinary, courteous way to address a woman, with none of the abruptness that “Woman” has in modern English. Jesus uses the same address to his mother in this Gospel. The traditional word is kept because English has no natural equivalent; “Madam” and “Dear woman” each add a tone the Greek lacks.

verse.text: Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you looking for?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him off, tell me where you have put him, and I will take him away.”
Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Hebrew, “Rabbouni!” (which means Teacher).
verse.note: The Greek word means “in the language of the Hebrews” and in this period could cover Aramaic as well as Hebrew proper. “Rabbouni” is usually identified as an Aramaic form, which is why some translations read “in Aramaic” here. In the Greek, Jesus also addresses Mary by the Semitic form of her name, Mariam.

verse.text: Jesus said to her, “Do not hold on to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”

note.term: Do not hold on to me

verse.note: The older rendering “Touch me not” suggests that Jesus forbids any contact. The Greek is a present-tense prohibition, which commonly means “stop doing” something already under way, and the verb can mean to take hold of or cling to. Most modern scholars and translations therefore understand Jesus to be telling Mary to let go of him, though the exact force of the reason he gives is still debated.

verse.text: Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord,” and that he had said these things to her.

When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were locked where the disciples were, for fear of the Jewish leaders, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, “Peace be with you.”
verse.note: The Greek says simply “the Jews,” the traditional rendering. The disciples behind the locked doors were themselves Jews, so the group they feared is the Jerusalem authorities who had just had Jesus put to death, and the translation makes that narrower reference explicit. Scholars are divided over how best to render this word in John; some prefer “Judeans,” others keep “Jews” throughout.

verse.text: Having said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
So Jesus said to them again, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, I also am sending you.”
Having said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.
verse.note: This verb occurs only here in the New Testament. It is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses when God breathes the breath of life into the first human (Genesis 2:7) and when breath enters the slain in Ezekiel’s vision of the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). A reader who knew those passages would have heard an act of new creation. The Greek has no object, and “on them” is supplied for English.

text.q: If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven them; if you retain anyone’s, they are retained.”

verse.note: Both “are forgiven” and “are retained” are perfect tenses in Greek, describing a settled state. Some interpreters press this to mean “they have already been forgiven,” so that the disciples announce what God has done; others take it simply as “they stand forgiven” once the disciples act. The grammar does not settle the question, and the rendering leaves it open.

verse.text: But Thomas, one of the Twelve, who was called the Twin, was not with them when Jesus came.
verse.note: Many translations leave the Greek word as a name, “Didymus.” It is the ordinary Greek word for a twin, and “Thomas” itself comes from the Aramaic word for twin, so John is giving his Greek readers the meaning of the name. The translation gives the meaning as some modern versions do. The text does not say whose twin he was.

verse.text: So the other disciples kept telling him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger into the mark of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will never believe.”
Eight days later his disciples were inside again, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were locked, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”
verse.note: Ancient counting normally included both the first and the last day. “Eight days later” therefore means a week later, on the following first day of the week, and some translations render it that way.

verse.text: Then he said to Thomas, “Bring your finger here and look at my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side. Do not be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, have you believed? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

note.traditional: Because you have seen me, you have believed.

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, so the sentence can be read as a question or as a statement (“Because you have seen me, you have believed”). The translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition used, which reads a question. The sense differs little either way: Thomas’s belief rests on sight, and the blessing is on those who believe without it.

verse.text: Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;
but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “the Christ.” Here the word is a title with the article, the claim that Jesus is the anointed king Israel expected, and not a second name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels while keeping “Christ” where it works as a name.

Manuscripts differ by one letter between two forms of the verb. One form (followed here) most naturally suggests “go on believing”; the other could suggest “come to believe.” The difference bears on whether the Gospel was written mainly to strengthen believers or to win new ones, but scholars caution that the tense alone cannot decide this, and the evidence is closely balanced.

verse.text: After these things Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way.
verse.note: This is another name for the Sea of Galilee, taken from the city of Tiberias on its western shore, which Herod Antipas founded and named for the emperor Tiberius. Only John’s Gospel uses this name in the New Testament.

verse.text: Simon Peter, Thomas called the Twin, Nathanael from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
Simon Peter said to them, “I’m going fishing.” They said to him, “We’re coming with you.” They went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing.
Just as morning was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; the disciples, however, did not know that it was Jesus.
So Jesus said to them, “Children, you don’t have any fish, do you?” They answered him, “No.”
verse.note: The Greek word means something eaten as a relish with bread, which in a fishing community normally meant fish. Some translations render it more generally as “anything to eat.” The form of the question in Greek expects the answer “no.”

verse.text: He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were not strong enough to haul it in because of the great number of fish.

So that disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he tied his outer garment around him, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.
verse.note: The word can mean fully naked, but it was also commonly used of someone wearing only an undergarment or a loincloth, as a laborer would. Most recent translations take it in this second sense here, though the older tradition has “naked.” Peter either put his outer garment on or, if he was already wearing it loosely, tucked it up to swim; the Greek allows both.

verse.text: But the other disciples came in the small boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from land, only about two hundred cubits away.
verse.note: A cubit was the length of a forearm, roughly eighteen inches or forty-five centimeters. Two hundred cubits is about one hundred yards, or ninety meters.

verse.text: When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire laid there, with fish lying on it, and bread.
verse.note: This word occurs in only one other place in the New Testament: John 18:18, where Peter stands warming himself at a charcoal fire while he denies Jesus three times. Many interpreters think the setting is meant to recall that scene before Peter is questioned three times.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish you have just caught.”
So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net to land, full of large fish, one hundred fifty-three of them; and though there were so many, the net was not torn.
verse.note: Since antiquity readers have proposed symbolic meanings for this number, but none has won general agreement. It may simply be the remembered count of an extraordinary catch.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “Come and have breakfast.” None of the disciples dared to ask him, “Who are you?” They knew it was the Lord.
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and the fish likewise.
This was now the third time Jesus was revealed to the disciples after being raised from the dead.
When they had eaten breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
verse.note: The Greek can mean “more than these other disciples love me,” “more than you love these others,” or “more than you love these things,” meaning the boat and nets. Most interpreters prefer the first, recalling Peter’s earlier claim to greater loyalty than the rest, but the wording does not settle it.

Jesus’ first two questions use the verb agapaō and his third uses phileō, while Peter answers with phileō each time. Some interpreters see a deliberate contrast between a higher and a lesser love. Most scholars today regard the change as stylistic variation, since this Gospel uses both verbs interchangeably elsewhere and the same passage also varies its words for “know,” “feed” and “sheep.” The translation follows the majority view and uses “love” for both.

verse.text: He said to him again, a second time, “Simon son of John, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Shepherd my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon son of John, do you love me?” Peter was grieved that he said to him the third time, “Do you love me?” and he said to him, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

text.q: Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were younger, you used to fasten your own belt and walk wherever you wanted; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will fasten a belt around you and take you where you do not want to go.”

verse.note: Stretching out the hands was an expression ancient writers used for crucifixion, in which the arms were spread on the crossbeam. The next verse confirms that the saying refers to Peter’s death, and early Christian tradition held that he was crucified in Rome, though the saying itself is not explicit about the manner.

verse.text: He said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. And after saying this, he said to him, “Follow me.”
Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following—the one who had leaned back against his chest at the supper and said, “Lord, who is it who is going to hand you over?”
verse.note: Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing someone into another’s custody, and the Gospels use the same word for what the priests and Pilate do to Jesus. The standard lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense; many scholars regard “betray” as an inference from context, though others defend it for Judas. This translation keeps “hand over” so the repeated word remains visible.

verse.text: So when Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about him?”
Jesus said to him, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”

So this saying spread among the brothers and sisters, that this disciple would not die. Yet Jesus did not say to him that he would not die, but, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?”
verse.note: The Greek plural was regularly used for a mixed group of men and women, and here it refers to the community of believers as a whole. Older versions have “brethren” or “brothers”; several recent ones have “brothers and sisters” or “the community.”

verse.text: This is the disciple who testifies about these things and who wrote them, and we know that his testimony is true.
verse.note: The “we” speaks for a group that vouches for the beloved disciple’s testimony, distinct from the disciple himself. Together with the apparent conclusion at the end of chapter 20, this leads many scholars to regard chapter 21 as an epilogue added by the disciple’s circle, though others hold it was part of the Gospel from the start. No surviving manuscript lacks the chapter.

verse.text: There are also many other things that Jesus did; if every one of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have room for the books that would be written.
